Over the last 6 years, the RSE community has grown rapidly in New Zealand and Australia. The RSE AUNZ steering committee was formally established in 2018 to support RSEs in New Zealand and Australia by raising awareness, advocating for RSEs and providing RSEs opportunities to connect through events, talks, and shared knowledge.
The committee has been working to provide opportunities to raise awareness of RSE at major events in the region, such as eResearch Australasia and eResearch New Zealand, doing outreach activities like presenting talks to grow the community, and planning next steps. While these efforts were what the community needed in its nascent stage, the community has evolved into a group of over 400 individuals and a renewed approach was needed.
This evolution has created limitations which include: 

Finite resources against growing needs

Competing priorities to progress goals

Lack of actionable key results for the high level goals

Documentation of the strategy to the community members and sector leaders

Difficulty in replacing outgoing steering committee members
Over the last year, while adapting to post pandemic life, the committee recognised an opportunity to address these limitations and pivot to an approach that could help serve our growing community better. The committee has worked on co-designing a strategy with the community which clearly defines goals and key results for the upcoming years. This strategy document received positive community feedback and it is publicly available via Figshare https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.21385392.v1. We will talk through the process involved in co-designing this strategy with the community.

title: Colouring Cities: From Prototype to Platform (with a little help from GitHub)
reasoning: The talk centers on a specific domain project (urban building stock data platform for cities), making it Research, but much of the content focuses on general GitHub features and software engineering practices for managing a large project, which is Software.
abstract:
The Colouring Cities Research Programme aims to develop open-source tools to facilitate knowledge and data sharing on national building stocks. It began with a prototype, Colouring London, and grew into an international collaboration, including cities such as Athens, Dresden, Bogotá and Jakarta. The aim is to create an open data platform that can be used for governance, planning and research, as well as tools to filter and explore the data (by ‘colouring’ buildings in different ways on an interactive map of the city).
When I joined the Project as an RSE, my responsibility was to oversee the transition from the Colouring London prototype to the new Core Platform, which was intended to facilitate easier and better collaboration between the various Colouring Cities projects. We also began to expand beyond a single city to the rest of the UK.
This transition was not without its challenges. Fortunately, my predecessors had made good use of GitHub, and encouraged the PIs to use it too. By using various GitHub features, we were able to manage this evolution and expansion of the project. This was my first experience using Git on such a large-scale project. I've learned a lot about various features of Organisations and Repositories, as well as features such as Issues, Projects, Discussions, Actions, Teams and more. 
In this talk, I will discuss some of these GitHub features, what it was like to use them, and how they enabled us to make this critical transition from the Prototype to Platform.

title: From prototype to production: developing a workflow for near-real time storm forecasting in Africa
reasoning: This is about productionizing domain-specific meteorological/storm forecasting software for Africa. The software is purpose-built for a specific scientific domain (meteorology), making it Research, with Software practices (workflow, scalability, monitoring) as secondary.
abstract:
Access to near real-time weather information is vital for decision-making, particularly in Africa, where unpredictability of weather patterns reduces confidence in longer-range forecasts.

FASTA (Forecasting AFrican STorms Application) aims to use satellite data to provide reliable information about storm rainfall in near real-time to enhance weather forecasts, help populations prepare for severe weather, and inform government and business decision-making.

Meteorological scientists at the University of Leeds developed prototype code to combine observational and nowcasting data produced by EUMETSAT NWCSAF software to identify rainfall and storm activity in a form that can be stored, retrieved and transferred efficiently and visualised in a mobile application front end or accessed via a web API.

This poster will explore the challenges encountered in translating the original research code into a robust and maintainable backend for the FASTA nowcasting mobile application and API, which make nowcasting products available for public consumption for the first time for most of Africa. In addition to setting up a processing workflow with minimal latency, these included technical considerations such as scalability, system monitoring and failover procedures.

title: Automating Data Flows in the Era of Big Data with Dpypeline
reasoning: Dpypeline is a general-purpose, customisable software for building data pipelines, applicable across domains, not tied to a specific research discipline.
abstract: In the era of big data, it is all the more necessary to implement robust practices to share and release data. As open science becomes gradually recognised as the way forward towards transparent and reproducible science, it is paramount to ensure that researchers have tools available to effectively transfer, transform, and analyse different datasets without sacrificing the time required for their scientific endeavours. As a step towards unified approaches to data processing and sharing, we present dpypeline, a software that allows building bespoke data pipelines to ease data processing. Dpypeline is a general, customisable, and extendable software that can automate the extraction, transformation, and updating of datasets. It aims to provide users with the flexibility necessary to build tailored data pipelines that meet the requirements of their applications. Dpypeline is written in Python and exposes a Python API and a command-line interface. The software core is designed using an extract-transform-load pattern, and current features include monitoring of triggering filesystem events, parallel streamlining of datasets, among other built-in methods that leverage the power of libraries such as Dask, Xarray, and Zarr. By automating data flows, this software can impact the availability of scientific data for analysis and reproducibility assessment.

title: An infrastructure as code template for data processing workflows on AWS
reasoning: A general-purpose IaC template for data processing pipelines on AWS, applicable across research domains—a cross-cutting tool/technique for RSEs.
abstract: To support spin-outs working with the UCL Centre for Digital Innovation as well as computationally intensive research projects, an open-source backend template has been built to encapsulate a generic data processing pattern. The data processing pattern, seen across research and industry use-cases, involves the ability to upload data, trigger a containerised processing pipeline, produce outputs and present the findings. The developed infrastructure that enables this processing pipeline leverages AWS services using best practice set out in the AWS Well Architect framework, drawing upon the modern serverless paradigm which ensures an efficient implementation from a cost and computational perspective. The template is developed in Terraform which is an open-source Infrastructure as Code (IaC) framework, and the codebase is modularised. The modularisation of the code allows for easy customisation by an end-user. This framework also allows for the easy translation of research into commercial applications. An overview on the AWS services used, lessons learned using Terraform and real use-cases will be presented.

title: I'm not paid to do that! 5 ways to have outsided impact through your work
reasoning: This talk focuses on RSE professional impact, career development, and raising the profile of research software engineering — squarely about people and the profession.
abstract: Are you tired of hearing that you need to do outreach, teach, or engage in other activities that seem impossible to fit into your already busy schedule? The good news is that you don't have to sacrifice your day-to-day work to have a real impact. In this talk, we'll explore five practical ways to make a difference through your job. From embracing open science to driving ecosystem change, we'll share real-world examples of what has worked (and what hasn't) to make scientific software more impactful. Join us to discover how you can have a meaningful impact through your work and help raise the profile of research software engineering.

title: Designing complex, reusable and scalable scientific workflows with Pydra
reasoning: Pydra is a general-purpose dataflow engine for scientific workflows, applicable across domains (despite neuroimaging origins). It's a cross-cutting tool for building reusable workflows.
abstract:
Designing scientific workflows is a challenging endeavour. They require composing multiple algorithms with different authorship, distribution channels (CLI, package, container) and necessary runtimes (Python, MATLAB). Such heterogeneity typically leads to semi-manual implementation, where scientists are expected to manage input and output files or interact with partial results. This is often time consuming, error-prone and makes experiments difficult to reproduce without adequate documentation or additional tooling.
This is the motivation behind `Pydra` — a general-purpose dataflow engine written in Python — designed with simplicity, reproducibility and scalability in mind. Born from a decade of experience building neuroimaging workflows with `Nipype` [1], `Pydra` provides flexible task semantics to facilitate composition of Python functions, shell commands and container processes. The resulting workflows also benefit from support for distributed execution, global caching and provenance tracking.
This walkthrough demonstrates how `Pydra` empowers the scientific community to build fully-automated, reusable and scalable workflows. First, the core components of `Pydra` [2] are introduced through simple task definitions in pure Python. More complex workflows are then showcased, with a mix of Python functions and shell command tasks, map-reduce semantics, and nested workflows. It concludes with advanced execution strategies and workflow customisation, including distributed computation, caching and container-based execution.
[1] Gorgolewski, Krzysztof, et al. "Nipype: a flexible, lightweight and extensible neuroimaging data processing framework in python." Frontiers in neuroinformatics (2011): 13.
[2] Jarecka, Dorota, et al. "Pydra - a flexible and lightweight dataflow engine for scientific analyses." Proceedings of the 19th python in science conference. Vol. 132. 2020.

title: Research, Software Engineering  Data Science for Social Good with DataKind: Lessons from the frontline
reasoning: This talk is about volunteering RSE/data science skills with charities for social good — a profession/community-facing initiative, with a case study illustrating impact. It's about people applying skills cross-domain rather than a specific scientific domain or general-purpose tool.
abstract:
DataKind UK are a charity that connects researchers, software engineers and data scientists from academia and industry with social change organisations like charities, letting them volunteer their time to research how the data an organisation holds can be used to transform their impact. This includes long-term engagement in DataCorps projects, as well as weekend-long DataDive hackathons. Volunteers search for patterns, and build pipelines and platforms to help answer questions the partners have. Volunteers can achieve serious real-world impact in a short time by applying their research and software engineering skills in a field with both a serious lack of, and need for, them.

In this talk, we will present an example of the lessons we’ve learned and the impact we’ve had from working with UK non-profits for 10 years. We will focus on one project in particular, working with a food bank to predict dependence on their services. The food bank struggled with how to best support people that came back 5 or 10 times to get food packages. These individuals weren't getting the support they needed from other services, and their problems weren't going away. The food bank had one support worker on hand to provide extra support - but they didn't know how to prioritise this support among the many people who came to the food bank daily. We helped with this, to ensure that those most in need got support the fastest. That might not sound like much - but for a small charity, that's big news!

title: CaRROT-CDM: An Open-Source Tool for Transforming Data for Federated Discovery in Health Research
reasoning: Tool purpose-built for health research data transformation to OMOP standard, serving a specific domain (health/medical research).
abstract:
Introduction 
Health Data are collected or repurposed for research in many organisations across the UK. These data are held in many formats and at many scales. Such data can contain information on biometric measurements, medical conditions, medical procedures, demographics, and prescribed medications with several coding systems in use. For GDPR compliance, data are stored securely and de-identified prior to use in research making sharing and standardisation more difficult.
The Observational Health Data Sciences and Informatics (OHDSI) program’s Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model (CDM) provides standard data objects and coding for health data.  
CaRROT-CDM 
Open-Source tools were developed to define mappings and transform data from numerous disparate organisations (the Data Partners) to the OMOP standard to allow federated data queries via the Health Data Research UK (HDR-UK) gateway. These tools are CaRROT-Mapper and CaRROT-CDM, with the latter being the focus here. 
CaRROT-CDM takes mapping information from the CaRROT-Mapper and source data as input. It produces OMOP CDM format data as output. The tool was designed to run in Data Partners’ compute environments, reducing the governance burden for transforming data to the common standard. Sensitive, identifiable data are never seen by the development team. 
Conclusions and Current Work 
The CaRROT-CDM tool is in use at Data Partner sites and has transformed over 20 COVID-19 and Pain data sets, so far, which are available for aggregated query via the HDR UK innovation gateway.
Current work is focussed on re-engineering and testing the software for scaling to population-level health data.

title: Collaborating on the Cloud: Creating an Organ Quality Scoring Tool
reasoning: This talk centers on a domain-specific tool for organ transplantation assessment, built for clinical/medical use with NHS data, though it discusses cloud infrastructure practices.
abstract:
Organ Quality Assessment is a cross-disciplinary project that aims to develop machine learning solutions to support transplant surgeons to assess the viability of organs for transplantation. The project will result in a web based tool which includes training data generation and near real time organ quality scoring. This talk will present the project background before exploring the cloud infrastructure used in detail. 
This project has involved our RSE team setting up Jupyter notebooks on the cloud to provide academic collaborators access to sensitive NHS data, which is restricted in where it can be stored and used. This allows both our RSEs and our research collaborators to interact with the controlled data in order to train and test machine learning algorithms. We will also discuss how rigorous audit trails and access policies were employed to meet regulatory and commercial requirements. 
We will outline lessons learned from combining web development, dev ops and machine learning in one project with both academic and clinical collaborators, as well as having to find solutions to working with restricted, sensitive data.

title: Tending the research software ecosystem garden: increasing interoperability  accessibility of diverse software packages and guiding users towards best practices via RSE-developed platforms
reasoning: The talk centers on QuantumBox, a platform built for crystallography, but the presenters explicitly frame it as illustrating transferable RSE approaches for integrating diverse software packages. It's a domain-specific tool with cross-cutting lessons.
abstract:
Due to the ever-increasing adoption of computer simulations in academic research, many research fields have sprouted diverse ecosystems of software packages. While these often implement advanced computational approaches, their use case and area of application can be fairly specific, making it desirable to combine several tools in a computational pipeline. 
However, the software dependencies of applications can be complex and sometimes mutually incompatible. They may also use bespoke, non-standard data formats or require advanced domain knowledge for their use. 
These aspects can pose significant challenges to a user's ability to employ these tools in their research, exchange data between different pieces of software and stitch them together in a coherent workflow. The researcher carries the additional burden of recording data provenance and ensuring reproducibility, either manually or via bespoke scripts and tools. 
As research software engineers, we have the opportunity to develop tools and platforms that provide the missing "glue" between different pieces of research software. Using the example of the emerging crystallographic platform "QuantumBox", we illustrate how research software engineering approaches can bring together a variety of highly disparate software packages, make them easier to access and use for inexperienced users and help users adopt best practices regarding data management and provenance tracking. While Quantum Box's area of application is in crystallography, the approaches and lessons learned are highly transferable to other fields. 
We present and discuss our approach and experience so far regarding design principles and software architecture, as well as the important aspect of community engagement.

title: TUG-RSE: Pulling Students into Research Software Engineering
reasoning: This session focuses on lowering entry barriers into the RSE profession for students, discussing community welcomeness and introducing a guide for undergraduates—clearly about people and the profession.
abstract:
Research Software engineering can often present a high entry barrier, especially for newcomers. Despite community efforts to create more entry-level positions, many individuals, especially students, still lack the required skill set or awareness of the field.

This session aims to delve deep into this issue and propose potential solutions to make the RSE community more welcoming. It would also introduce “‘The Undergraduate's Guide To Research Software Engineering’ (TUG-RSE)”, a project aimed to address this very challenge.

This session welcomes RSEs at all career stages and anyone with a keen interest in research software. The goal is to facilitate an open dialogue, while gathering valuable audience feedback and suggestions.

title: FAIRsharing Assistant - The FAIRsharing wizard
reasoning: FAIRsharing is a cross-cutting, profession-wide infrastructure for FAIR data discovery, serving researchers and RSEs across all disciplines. It's a tool but its purpose is community/policy infrastructure (FAIR principles, data stewardship).
abstract:
Announcing the FAIRsharing Assistant, a new component of FAIRsharing designed to guide the research data community towards a customised set of databases, standards and policies relevant to them, and to help enable FAIR data.
FAIRsharing is a curated, informative and educational resource on data and metadata standards, inter-related to databases and data policies, across all disciplines. FAIRsharing guides consumers to discover, select and use these resources with confidence, and producers to make their resource more discoverable, more widely adopted and cited.

FAIRsharing promotes the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable) Principles, and therefore enables FAIR data, by promoting the value and use of data and metadata standards, and their use by databases.
One such tool is the FAIRsharing Assistant, a friendly Graphical User Interface, which has been designed using VueJs, D3Js, javascript to offer personalised guidance to those in research and in research support roles (e.g. researchers, developers, curators, policymakers, data stewards, librarians, standards development organisations, societies) to discover standards and repositories in FAIRsharing. The Assistant also signposts other FAIR-enabling resources to aid the user in the creation and discovery of FAIR data.

title: GPU code optimization and automatic performance tuning made easy with Kernel Tuner
reasoning: Kernel Tuner is a general-purpose auto-tuning tool for GPU code, applicable across domains, focused on software optimization techniques.
abstract:
Graphics Processing Units (GPUs) have revolutionized the HPC landscape. The first generation of exascale supercomputers is currently being built, and most of these systems will have GPUs as their main computing platform. The performance of GPU applications strongly depends on how the software has been optimized for the hardware. There are many different implementations and code optimizations to consider that can also be parameterized, creating vast search spaces that are infeasible to search by hand. As such, automated performance tuning (auto-tuning) techniques are crucial to optimize such applications. 

In this tutorial, you will learn how to use Kernel Tuner, an easy-to-use tool for auto-tuning GPU code using simple Python scripts. Kernel Tuner supports OpenCL, CUDA, C++, and Fortran. We take a step-by-step approach to explain the auto-tuning basics, building up to more complex search spaces with many tunable parameters and inter-dependencies.  

We cover a wide range of topics from the basics of GPU code optimization, to using advanced search space optimization strategies to accelerate the auto-tuning process. Participants are welcome to bring their own code for the exercises, but we also provide plenty of code examples.

title: Reducing the overhead of coupled machine learning models between Python and Fortran
reasoning: Presents general-purpose Fortran-Python interoperability libraries for ML coupling, applicable across many scientific domains (geophysics, plasma, CFD, chemistry). While tested on an atmospheric simulation, the artifact is a cross-cutting tool.
abstract:
Machine learning (ML) is increasingly used within larger computational projects to achieve higher computational and/or predictive performance.

This typically results in the challenge of language interoperation: Python is popular for building ML models due to libraries like PyTorch and TensorFlow, whilst Fortran is used for many large, high-performance, scientific codes. Notable examples of fields commonly using large Fortran codes include geophysical science, plasma physics, computational fluid dynamics, and chemistry. Since these two languages lack native interoperation, aligning the two requires care.
Interoperability libraries exist, such as forpy, to allow communication between the languages. They establish native Python types that are accessible from Fortran and require restructuring of data when exchanging information. They also require the maintenance and linking of a suitable Python environment. In this work, we ask, is this method the best approach?

We present alternative approaches for TensorFlow and PyTorch that avoid direct use of Python. We have produced Fortran libraries to access the underlying ML codebase via an Application Programming Interface (API), with data stored in shared memory between the two. For PyTorch this accesses a TorchScript model, whilst TensorFlow involves code-generation of a Fortran module.
We test these approaches in the context of coupling an ML model to an atmospheric simulation to replace a physics-based parameterisation. Early tests indicate speedup of up to 4x when compared to the forpy approach. Our libraries are open-source and well-documented, with examples to guide users with a wide variety of possible use-cases across the range of fields noted above.

title: AntigenApp: building a web application for nanobody analysis using a DevOps approach
reasoning: AntigenApp is built for a specific domain (nanobody/antibody research), but the talk's focus is on the DevOps approach, Kubernetes, CI/CD, and cloud-native lessons applicable to any RSE building web applications.
abstract:
Nanobodies are a small form of antibody which, due to their small size and low chemical complexity, hold significant promise as diagnostic and therapeutic agents. The experimental pipeline for nanobody production involves multiple stages and experiment modalities. At the Rosalind Franklin Institute, scientists were finding it challenging to capture all the relevant experimental data and metadata in a way that is searchable and shareable among teams and collaborators. To solve this, we built AntigenApp, a web application which functions both as a database and specialised bioinformatics platform.
As a small team of research software engineers, we adopted a DevOps approach, whereby RSEs are responsible for both development and operations of software, leveraging automation for efficiency. We utilise a modular technology stack centred around a Postgres database, a backend Python/Django web application, and a React-based frontend. The application runs on Kubernetes using a continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) approach.
In this talk, I will discuss the successes and challenges we’ve faced in developing and running AntigenApp across its whole lifecycle, including why we chose a “cloud native” technology stack, how we decided when to “pivot” in terms of technologies used and refactoring, and lessons learned on deploying to Kubernetes including security, performance, monitoring errors, and streamlining the update process using “gitops”. We hope our experience is useful to other application developers using or considering “cloud native” application development on Kubernetes.

title: Modern Training for Modern Fortran
reasoning: Panel about Fortran training for RSEs—centers on training/curriculum and community feedback, but Fortran is a cross-cutting general-purpose language skill. Training falls under Community per the scheme.
abstract: Although Fortran’s origins date back to the 1950s, the language is still widely used by the scientific community. Its strength lies in numerical and parallel computation, so it is often used to build efficient, complex software, designed to run on high-performance computers. Despite its widespread usage, there is a lack of suitable training for RSEs and other users, particularly when it comes to best practices with modern Fortran. Furthermore, many Fortran programmers deal with legacy code written in old versions and using outdated software practices. Hence, there is a pressing need to create a common, modernised set of Fortran programming practices that help the RSE community to write better scientific software. During this panel we will showcase our current training, and ideas for improvement and future training. We invite RSEs to provide feedback and suggestions to guide future material throughout the panel, focusing on a range of themes such as best practice, modern Fortran, and Fortran for HPC.

title: How to use and contribute to a software sustainability dashboard
reasoning: A workshop about a general-purpose software sustainability dashboard tool, applicable across research software projects. Sustainability tooling is explicitly cross-cutting (Software), though it touches community practices.
abstract:
The need for sustainable software is well established in the research software engineering community. Developing sustainable software ensures that your project will last beyond your current funding and make a sustained impact. The precise meaning of sustainable software remains somewhat vague, with many different contributing factors, the importance of which can vary according to the user/use case; e.g. code quality assurance, contributor base, user support and engagement, licencing model. In addition, existing metrics such as technical debt are likely to be correlated to software sustainability. Keeping track of these disparate factors becomes very difficult when managing a portfolio of software. To address this in our own practice we developed a single sustainability dashboard for our own distributed project (SciKit-Surgery) that summarises a selection relevant metrics and factors measures of software sustainability onto a single dynamic webpage.

We are currently producing a publicly available version which will allow developers to configure their own list of projects and criteria by which to compare sustainability amongst them and learn from best practice. During this workshop we will discuss different aspects of software sustainability. We will compare existing practice across a selection of open-source software projects, and ask what measures of sustainability translate into lasting success. We will invite delegates to share their own experience of developing sustainable software. We will then work with participants to submit their existing open-source projects to our dashboard and optionally to contribute their own metrics to the dashboard.

title: State of Code Quality in RSE: an Empirical Study of Software Development in Different Research Areas
reasoning: Empirical study comparing RSE practices across research domains to industry SE, focused on the profession and its practices rather than a specific tool or scientific question.
abstract:
What is good software? This is one of the major questions the software engineering community has been confronting for decades. There have been various approaches and ultimately very different answers to this question. However, the SE community always treated software development as a – in general – similar activity for all areas of application, ignoring the difference between industry software and research software.
As software becomes ever more essential in modern research of all kinds that, ultimately, affect our society, economy, and politics, high quality software is inevitable. But what are the actual differences between RSE and traditional SE? To which extent does research software already employ SE techniques? What are concerns that are only relevant to research? Do all these findings apply to RSE in general, or are certain practices more relevant in particular research fields than in others?
In this talk, we will present insights from an empirical investigation on how software is developed in different research domains today and what shortcomings the development has regarding relevant software quality and SE best practices. We demonstrate results gathered from interviews, surveys, and repository analysis of many research projects of different fields, compare them to industry level software engineering and evaluate which of these “traditional” metrics and practices are important to research software as well and which are only industry-specific, as well as which other concerns RSE has that are not shared with industry SE.

title: Using ReFrame for reproducible and portable performance benchmarking
reasoning: ReFrame is a general-purpose benchmarking/regression testing framework applicable across HPC users and domains, fitting Software.
abstract:
Testing and benchmarking software on HPC systems is still often manual and time consuming which makes porting and comparing performance across different systems time consuming and error prone. In this workshop we show how building and running benchmarks can be automated across many different HPC configurations using ReFrame. ReFrame is widely used for regression testing by HPC services from small group clusters up to the largest supercomputers in the world (including the UK national supercomputer, ARCHER2) and is being used by the ExCALIBUR UK exascale programme for cross-platform benchmarking. This workshop will introduce using ReFrame for the automation of benchmarking and collecting performance data. We will introduce how ReFrame is configured and how ReFrame tests can be constructed independently of system configuration and deployed on multiple systems with low overhead. Participants will learn to write a simple ReFrame class, and run it on HPC platforms. Following the workshop, attendees should have enough knowledge to start using ReFrame in their day-to-day activities. The workshop will be taught by ARCHER2 service staff and the developers from the ExCALIBUR benchmark activity who have experience of using ReFrame in production.

Participants can bring their own applications for benchmarking and work on a remote system that is relevant for them, or work locally on a Linux laptop. We will provide access to ARCHER2 and an example application to work on for participants who do not wish to bring their own.

title: Exploiting bind(c) to run modern Fortran on modern hardware, economics be damned!
reasoning: This talk discusses a Fortran compiler interoperability technique (bind(c)) used in CFD code development, but the focus is on a general software engineering approach to enable modern Fortran with GPU support, applicable to others facing similar problems. While CFD is the context, the technique is cross-cutting.
abstract: Despite rumours to the contrary, Fortran enables writing software that is abstracted, high-level and clean, using modern development practices such as generic interfaces. However, due to economies of scale, support for modern standards is not guaranteed across Fortran compiler vendors as might be expected based on the C++ compiler ecosystem. This may contribute to the perception of Fortran as a legacy language. We have recently experienced this situation during the ASiMoV-CCS CFD code development effort. A key design goal of ASiMoV-CCS is to avoid hard dependencies, such as a specific linear algebra backend. We achieve this through a combination of generic interfaces and submodules, with a particular implementation selected at link time. This enables developers to provide alternative implementations by coding to match the interface. More importantly however, the higher-level scientific code remains independent of implementation. Unfortunately, the features that our design requires were not well supported by the currently available NVHPC nvfortran compilers, limiting the ASiMoV-CCS development options for the GPU ecosystem. We joined the recent UK National GPU hackathon in the hope of finding a solution to this problem. With guidance from our mentors from NVIDIA, we implemented a solution based on bind(c), which ensures the compiler creates C compatible objects. This enabled using gfortran (supporting high-level abstractions) as the primary compiler and linking a small subset of our code developed for GPU offload and compiled with nvfortran. This talk will present the approach taken in the hope it proves useful to others facing similar problems.

title: Over 180 years of research data and its software: An ongoing history of BGS Geomagnetism.
reasoning: Case study of geomagnetism research software at BGS — software built for a specific scientific domain (geomagnetism/geoscience), making it Research, though it touches on cross-cutting legacy software maintenance challenges.
abstract:
The strength and direction of the Earth’s magnetic field has been systematically measured in the UK since 1840.

The British Geological Survey (BGS) is the UK’s premier provider of objective and authoritative geoscientific data. The organisation was founded in 1835 and is a repository for datasets such as those held by the geomagnetism unit that are long-standing, uninterrupted, and continuously recorded. The data has been subject to processing and analysis long before the beginning of the "Information Age".

Paper notebooks have given way to computer disks and software has revolutionised data analysis. What was once cutting edge becomes obsolete. But legacy remains for long-established datasets and the associated software that manages, analyses and shares that data. The past affects present and future for researchers, and the institutions and RSEs that support them.
Technologies will rise and fall. Standards may be formulated but are sometimes usurped. Policies and regulations move and shift.

How do researchers and RSEs manage and future proof this ever changing landscape?
Here we present a case study of an enduring science project, the evolution of its systems and software, and the challenges that its legacy and its future brings for the people who maintain it.

title: Research assessment is the dull sounding, but vital missing element from true recognition for Research Software Engineers.
reasoning: This talk is about recognition, research assessment, and the RSE profession—centered on people and policy rather than a specific tool or scientific domain.
abstract:
The RSE community has achieved huge success in gaining recognition for the RSE role in the UK and around the world. We have widespread recognition with researchers, senior management in universities and research organisations, and with policymakers throughout academia, funders and government. The research world has changed rapidly. Yet the way in which we judge what "success" means in research has stayed stubbornly unchanged. Recognition for RSEs cannot be said to have been truly achieved until our work is viewed equally to other contributions to research.
In this talk, I will present the current status of recognition for research software and how the results from the latest REF show an ever-increasing focus on publications. Based on my interviews with REF managers and others involved in research assessment, I will describe the competing pressures placed on universities as the source of this myopic view on success. I will finish by describing some of the activities and campaigns that are working to broaden the community's interpretation of success and summarise some of the breakthroughs they have made in support of RSEs and other vital-but-unrecognised roles.

title: Enabling Science with Marine Autonomous Systems in Remote Offline Environments
reasoning: Talk centers on a software solution purpose-built for marine science operations (controlling Marine Autonomous Systems for oceanographic research), tied specifically to the marine/oceanography domain.
abstract:
The National Oceanography Centre hosts the National Marine Equipment Pool which includes Europe’s largest operating fleet of MAS (Marine Autonomous Systems). Our fleet is operated in a wide range of marine environments across the globe and is used to collect data from coast to deep ocean. The variety of operational areas and increasing complexity of MAS makes planning and executing successful missions increasingly challenging. Our fleet is comprised of commercial off the shelf and purpose-built in-house systems. Such systems have been traditionally piloted over-the-horizon where pilots command control MAS via satellite communications. In this presentation we will briefly explore the capabilities of our solution to unify the operation of our MAS fleet and how pilots can plan missions, review near-real-time data and control MAS from any internet connected device including exploring the technology stack behind the scenes.
Then, we will navigate through our journey of adapting our web-based over-the-horizon command and control solution to operate fully offline from ship or shore from any location. We will present how this solution was used to support our long-range MAS Autosub Long Range (affectionately known as Boaty McBoatface) during a deployment under a West Antarctic ice sheet from an icebreaker ship during the 2021/2022 Antarctic summer.
We will conclude by presenting the results of the project’s first year in action in the context of science campaigns and ambitious engineering trials. Additionally, we will briefly outline our future development plans and how our solution will support future science expeditions across the globe.

title: Embedding a Right to Replicate in RSE practices
reasoning: This talk discusses a policy/principle (Right to Replicate) addressing vendor lock-in and sustainability across RSE practices, which is profession-wide and cross-organisation policy oriented, though it also touches on cross-cutting software practices.
abstract: As RSEs, we are constantly faced with choices to avoid vendor lock-in, in some form or another, and think about the sustainability and reusability of our outputs. This talk will introduce the Right to Replicate as an example of both how the issue of vendor lock-in has been addressed for infrastructure projects by outlining specific infrastructure commitments when developing digital goods, and how setting such values at an organisation or team level can lubricate operational activities. Lastly, the talk will invite reflection on where a Right to Replicate could apply to less infrastructure-centred projects.

title: Project Bluebird: AI research in air traffic control and the role of research software engineers
reasoning: This talk centers on a specific domain research project (AI for Air Traffic Control), describing both the domain-specific software work and the RSE team's approaches. Primary is Research (domain-specific application), with secondary Community (RSE team practices/role).
abstract:
Project Bluebird is a multi-institutional research project aiming to apply human-centered AI to the complex task of Air Traffic Control (ATC). The project, an EPSRC funded Prosperity partnership between NATS, The Alan Turing Institute and the University of Exeter, covers a range of technical challenges: from developing physics-based probabilistic models of aircraft trajectories, creating machine learning systems that collaborate with humans to make ATC decisions, and to the design of tools that promote safe, explainable, and trustworthy use of AI in ATC.

Given the ambitious aims of the project, and the extensive range of domain specific knowledge required to achieve these aims, delivering a quality software solution is a major challenge. Research software engineers (RSEs) have both expertise in professional software development practices and domain speciﬁc knowledge enabling them to produce reliable, eﬃcient and maintainable software for research.

In this talk we will discuss the latest updates from the project and the challenges our RSE team have faced working on such a complex, multi-disciplinary project. We will present approaches to developing research software that we have successfully utilised to date, and the benefits that a diversely experienced team of RSEs can bring when creating cutting-edge, AI solutions.

title: The Challenges of Maintaining an Active 60-year-old Library
reasoning: Talk about maintaining a long-standing mathematical software library, focusing on RSE practices like testing, documentation, building, distribution, and licensing. While HSL is for numerical linear algebra, the talk centers on cross-cutting software engineering practices for legacy code modernization.
abstract:
Is HSL a legacy code? What would it take to make it feel “modern”?

The HSL library (https://www.hsl.rl.ac.uk/) was started as the Harwell Subroutine Library in 1963 and is the oldest mathematical software library to be in continual use. Originally developed for use by researchers at UK Atomic Energy Authority (UKAEA) Harwell, packages have been added to the library as research outputs and can be removed when usage, research interest, or competition dictates. The whole library has always been written in Fortran and the oldest codes in the library that have not been archived are just over 30 years old.

Maintaining such a library has become increasingly complicated as RSE debt has built up in recent years when compared to what might be expected of “modern” software libraries. This maintenance must be balanced against the group’s interests in developing new research in numerical linear algebra.

I’ll talk about why I think the library is still used and some of the key differences we’ve seen when comparing the current library against an ideal software package including the approach to testing, documentation, building, and distributing. Additionally, I’ll cover our issues with licensing and the direction of the project in the next few years with an emphasis on the RSE work required to get there and why now.

title: International RSE collaboration with the Institute of Computing for Climate Science and the Virtual Earth System Research Institute
reasoning: This describes a domain-specific RSE group (ICCS) collaborating with climate science teams, focusing on the group model, RSE development, and international collaboration. It's primarily about people/profession/community structures, though tied to climate science domain.
abstract:
The Virtual Earth Science Research Institute (VESRI) is made up of several large international science teams of about thirty researchers in each. They study topics essential in climate science including sea ice dynamics, gravity wave parameterisations, machine learning in multi-scale modes and a novel land ecosystem model. The Institute of Computing for Climate Science (ICCS) is domain specific, international form of RSE group designed to (in the first instance) collaborate with VESRI teams by combining research software engineering, programming language research, machine learning and data science techniques.
The ICCS supports the VESRI teams by collaborating as RSEs on software projects, consulting, running training events (e.g. Summer School) in the UK and as side events at other conferences like WCRP OSC, and hosting relevant conferences like Climate Informatics. We help with typical RSE concerns such as version control, testing, continuous integration, packaging, documentation, as well as more specific topics like machine learning, coupling, IO library API design, and GPU programming. An important goal of the ICCS is the development of RSEs themselves and the institute is also partnered with a broad program of international Virtual Institutes for Scientific Software (VISS).
This poster introduces the team, the work, the group model and highlights some recent scientific results.

title: From Microscope to Metadata Catalogue: Creating Infrastructure to support OpenFAIR data in a scientific institute.
reasoning: This talk describes data infrastructure built for a specific biomedical research institute (Rosalind Franklin Institute) handling Cryo-EM and proteomics data. While the technologies (Ceph, Scicat, HPC/Cloud) are general, the context and motivation are domain-specific scientific data management.
abstract:
The Rosalind Franklin Institute is a new centre dedicated to fighting disease from protein to organ level. It is composed of 5 themes including Artificial Intelligence and Informatics and has put Open FAIR data at the core of its principles. The Franklin produces a range of data: from multi-terabyte Cryo-EM datasets to millions of small proteomics spectra, which is analysed by users with a range of computing knowledge.  In 2022, the data output of the Franklin increased 5-fold in the space of 6 months. This prompted the need to refactor our infrastructure to provide a scalable, flexible platform for transferring, archiving and processing these vast amounts of data.
This talk focusses on how we built the 2nd phase of the data infrastructure using a mixture of open-source and licensed technology. We have built a methodology to move processing between Cloud and HPC. We are leveraging Ceph Echo object store for our data and are using Scicat to catalogue our metadata.  We will discuss how the Franklin aims to move towards automated processing and how the technology we have implemented will make this possible.

title: A continuous integration workflow for HPC using Singularity, HPC-Rocket and FieldCompare
reasoning: This describes a general-purpose CI/CD workflow for HPC using cross-cutting tools (Singularity, HPC-Rocket, FieldCompare, GitLab CI), applicable across research domains.
abstract:
Human error is a common cause of bugs and defects in software and can be very costly in terms of time, resources, and reputation. Automating scientific workflows can reduce the risk of human error by performing repetitive and time-consuming tasks with greater accuracy and consistency than humans. This can improve the overall quality of the software, reduce the time and effort required for testing and deployment, and help to ensure that the software meets the required quality standards. Furthermore, automation can add to the reproducibility of scientific results as all the necessary steps to generate them need to be recorded in a script, making workflows easily repeatable. 
Automation can however be very challenging in the context of high-performance computing, as users lack the necessary permissions on the HPC system as well as the manual work required to submit and monitor jobs.
In this walkthrough, we present a continuous integration workflow using Singularity, HPC Rocket, and FieldCompare in a GitLab CI pipeline to automate the process of providing executable containers, deploying them to the HPC system, and continuously verifying computational results against trusted reference data.

title: The Met Office and the climate model evaluation community: a story of collaborations, challenges and conversations
reasoning: This talk centers on a climate-domain tool (ESMValTool) but the focus is on the Met Office's adoption journey, open-source community building, governance, and workshops — i.e., people and profession aspects. However, the tool is domain-specific (climate model evaluation), making Research a strong secondary.
abstract:
Climate model evaluation is a crucial step in the development and improvement of climate modelling capability. In 2020, the Met Office (the UK's national meteorological service) made the decision to replace their bespoke, in-house tools used to perform climate model evaluation with an open-source, community driven tool called ESMValTool. Adopting ESMValTool at the Met Office enables all the benefits of using open source software, including collaborating with the wider climate model evaluation and analysis community, but it also comes with challenges. The Met Office journey so far includes:
completing technical analysis to support the strategic commitment to adopt ESMValTool
facilitating the development of a governance structure
making contributions to the community, including hosting an ESMValTool workshop last October
Come along to hear more about our journey and what makes ESMValTool a successful open-source community!

title: Where is all the research software? An analysis of software in UK academic repositories.
reasoning: This is about software recognition policy, institutional repositories, and how academia treats software as research output - a profession-wide infrastructure/policy issue. It's also research analysis itself.
abstract:
There has been a steep decline in numbers of research software submissions to the UK's Research Excellence Framework (REF) from 2008 to 2021, but there has been no investigation into whether and how the official academic Institutional Repositories (IRs) have affected the low return rates. In what we believe to be the first such census of its kind, we queried the online repositories of over 180 UK universities. Our findings show that the prevalence of software within UK Academic IRs is incredibly low. A minority contain software as recognised academic output.  Of greater concern, we found that a large majority of repositories cannot record software as a type of research output and that several Universities appeared to have removed software as a defined type from default settings of their repository. We also explored potential correlations, such as being a member of the Russell group, but found no correlation between these metadata and prevalence of records of software. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings with regards to the lack of recognition of software as a discrete research output in institutions, despite the opposite being mandated by funders, and we make recommendations for changes in policies and operating procedures.
Please note this is a presentation of work, along with expansion results, that is under review for PeerJ Computer Science.

title: My Octopus Teacher: Lessons learned in eight years of building web apps for the Autonomous Underwater Vehicles used in Oceanography
reasoning: This talk is about a team's experience building software for a specific domain (oceanography/AUVs), focusing on team organization, agile practices, and lessons learned. While the application is domain-specific (Research), the talk's emphasis is on transferable team/workflow practices and lessons for other RSE teams, which leans Community.
abstract:
In 2016, the Oceanids programme began. It was funded by the UK Government, with the aim of increasing national oceanographic research capability through the development of Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV) hardware and software.
We work within the software side, on the "Command and Control" (C2) project. Our goal is to create an intuitive control interface for all the AUVs in our fleet here at the National Oceanography Centre (NOC), and reduce the barriers to using AUVs in research projects through developing useful APIs and standardizing data formats for the research communities.
Our funding and workload comes both from academia and commercial interests.  We are often writing experimental code and collaborating with researchers, but to strict deadlines - sea-going expeditions must be planned far in advance and it can be very costly to postpone putting things in the water.
We started as several junior developers eight years ago with cursory knowledge of "scrum" and "git flow". Today, we are a team of eight with a well-defined development workflow and an application being used daily by NOC's AUV operators and scientists. Our team has been making efforts to teach development practices we've learned to other groups at NOC. Our mascot is an Octopus.
This talk tells the story of how we've grown C2 as an agile project in this environment. We'll present the ways in which we've organised our team, our work and our communication - what we tried, and what we've found works for us, at home and at sea.

title: How do we design and deliver sustainable digital research education
reasoning: Workshop on inclusive education and EDIA in research computing training — about people, profession, and curriculum design.
abstract:
There is known disparity between the diversity of undergraduate cohorts and that of researchers in many fields.
In STEM fields there are known diversity issues from the age of 11 upwards.
As research computing professionals we are also often research computing educators.
How do we design learning experiences for researchers and research students that do not further embed these issues?
In this workshop we will explore sustainable education in the context of research computing educating and steps we can take to improve EDIA and embed social justice.

title: The Other Kind of Accessible: removing software barriers for disabled researchers and RSEs
reasoning: This talk is about accessibility for disabled people as a profession-wide concern, addressing inclusion, attitudes, and practices across the RSE community. While it mentions technical practices like accessibility testing, the core focus is on the people/profession dimension.
abstract:
When researchers and RSEs use the word "accessible" while discussing their work, it is usually in the context of making data and software more openly available. But there is another meaning of “accessible” that is often overlooked: the ability for disabled people to understand and use the data and software that are produced.
At least 15% of people worldwide are disabled, yet there is little discussion in RSE spaces of how to create accessible research tools and outputs, and people often don't realise when they are creating barriers. As a result, many disabled researchers are unable to do their research effectively, because the tools they need to use do not meet their needs. Disabled RSEs may even be expected to work on software which they cannot use themselves. 
At The Carpentries, we are working to improve the accessibility of our web infrastructure, events, and organisational culture. I will draw examples from this experience in this talk, where I will discuss how we are all responsible for the accessibility of our outputs, and what steps we as RSEs can take to improve. This includes technical steps like learning best practices and incorporating accessibility tests into our workflows, as well as psychological steps like changing our collective attitude toward disability and accessibility.

title: And then there were users: Designing and implementing governance for open research software projects
reasoning: This talk is about governance for open research software projects, focusing on community structures, decision-making, and project sustainability—a profession-wide concern. While it uses CFF as a case study, the focus is on governance practices applicable across RSE community.
abstract: As RSEs, we aim to develop research software in a way that makes it reusable by others. Sometimes, the community of users and contributors around our reusable software grows quickly, while the number of people maintaining the software stays the same, and is often very small to begin with. In this situation, our decisions about the software and the project may affect many more people than anticipated. This calls for a formalization and communication of how we make and enforce decisions within the project, i.e., governance. When we devise governance, there may be many open questions, some of them rather philosophical: What is the actual mission of the project, what are its aims and scope? What are the foundational principles of our project, especially for interacting with different roles in our community? What requirements do we need our model of governance to support? Practical questions follow: What organizational structures do we need? How should these structures interact with each other? What are the processes we need, and how do we implement them? Who gets to decide what? What are the risks, and what do we do if something goes wrong? How can we ensure that governance does not add too much to the already heavy workloads of the people that are involved? And finally: How do we document and enforce all of this? In this talk, we share experiences from recent work to design and implement governance for the Citation File Format project, and some challenges we faced.

title: DAFNI: Extending input data sources for a model workflow platform
reasoning: DAFNI is a platform built specifically for national infrastructure research (power, water, transport, etc.), and the talk discusses extending its data management for that domain. The acid test applies: can't explain without naming the infrastructure research domain.
abstract:
We present ongoing work on expanding the data management capabilities of an established workflow platform to accommodate a wider range of data sources. 
The Data & Analytics Facility for National Infrastructure (DAFNI) enables collaborative research into the resilience and sustainability of national infrastructure such as power networks, transportation, telecommunications, water, population dynamics and much more. DAFNI holds its users’ data and allows them to run models together in a system-of-systems approach.  Thus, the platform provides a neutral space for data and models to be shared and used to explore new scenarios together - without needing direct access to the code - and then kept as a legacy space, which can be accessed by stakeholders after the end of research projects. The target audience is the domain expert: government (including OFGEM, OFCOM, OFWAT etc), infrastructure asset owners, economists, insurance, and researchers at universities. 
Data has traditionally all been held in DAFNI’s repository where versions and provenance are tracked.  As the platform has grown, we have identified needs for (a) large (>50gb) datasets from external sources such as NERC data centres (to enable climate modelling) or external clouds, and (b) data of higher security levels (to enable research on infrastructure that is commercially sensitive or raises national security concerns). In addition to the “plumbing” of moving data around, the challenges include versioning and provenance of external data, and trying to make data management user friendly for the non-technical users.

title: Fairy WANDS for Fusion
reasoning: WANDS is a framework built specifically for fusion experiment data transfer needs (tokamak intershot analysis), making it domain-specific research software, though the framework itself is fairly general data streaming infrastructure.
abstract:
Modern supercomputers provide the necessary computing power to analyze data produced by large scientific experiments. However, since data generation and compute sites are typically not co-located, a need to transfer the data arises. This can quickly become a bottleneck, especially when ad-hoc analysis of experimental data is essential. One such use-case is nuclear fusion.

Magnetically confined fusion is one of the two main forms of artificially produced nuclear fusion. One of the most promising types of fusion reactors is a tokamak. Tokamaks are pulsed reactors; instead of running continuously, they run individual reactions known as shots. To be a viable concept for energy generation, it is imperative that reactors can respond quickly and correctly to chaotic plasma events to avoid losing confinement. This requires analyzing data gathered from previous shots. To keep the intershot analysis time as short as possible, the compute power of modern supercomputers is necessary, creating the need to transfer data across Wide Area Networks efficiently.

We are presenting the Wide Area Network Data Streaming (WANDS) framework currently under development. WANDS provides a flexible, user-friendly, and efficient implementation of a server-client model to request subsets of data for processing. The WANDS client has a Python interface for direct integration into data analysis scripts. A lightweight C++ server component on the data production site serves these requests. Communication is facilitated using ADIOS2. A client-side cache further accelerates subsequent requests for previously transferred data.

title: Using SYCLomatic to Make GPU Code Cross-Platform
reasoning: Cross-platform GPU porting tool (SYCLomatic) is general-purpose HPC tooling applicable across domains.
abstract:
High Performance Computing systems are becoming more heterogenous, with CPUs and GPUs from different vendors in different combinations. If a research group applies for time on a large HPC system, there is a likelihood that the CPU and GPU combination might not match the programming model their software was originally written in. The vast majority existing code is written in one programming model (CUDA) for one vendor’s GPU hardware. 

SYCL is an open standard, cross-platform portability layer for C++ to target diverse CPU, GPU and other accelerators. 

But what happens if you aren’t starting from scratch and need to port an existing CUDA code? That’s where SYCLomatic comes in. SYCLomatic is an open source, source to source translation tool that automates nearly all of the of the tedious work of translating. 

In this walk through we will introduce the tool, demonstrate a simple example, and then some more complex examples that show what happens when the tool isn’t able to translate a code structure and what is left for the porter to do by hand.

title: Snapshot on King’s Digital Lab Mission and Activities 2022-25: communicating the significance of RSE in a research-intensive HEI context
reasoning: This talk is about defining and communicating the mission of an RSE team/hub within a university context, focusing on the RSE profession, team identity, and institutional positioning rather than a specific tool or research domain.
abstract: This talk aims to present the Mission and Activities document produced by King’s Digital Lab (KDL) in collaboration with Faculty senior management last year. KDL is an RSE research facility at the Faculty of Arts and Humanities, King’s College London (UK). The document is the result of a light review process spurred by the Faculty to restate KDL’s mission and its “doing, enabling and planning” activities (inclusive of operational overheads and Research Services Catalogue). While the document is specific to KDL and mainly fulfils the internal function to communicate our remit to stakeholders and allocate resources, the talk will contextualize it within RSE references (e.g. DOI 10.1109/MS.2020.2973362) as well as similar efforts and good practices initiated by other RSE hubs across the country (e.g. Newcastle University, University College London, Alan Turing Institute, University of Edinburgh) and beyond. The main scope of the talk would be to foreground the agency RSE teams can exercise in defining and reviewing mission and activities following an engineering ethos. The aim is also to showcase how such an exercise can contribute to navigating challenges related to conflicting pressures for RSE teams, while striving for alignment to institutional strategies and responses to other external factors (e.g. funding, policies). The objective is to inspire discussions on the mechanisms via which the significance of RSE contribution to a research-intensive Higher Education Institution can be communicated and adapted responsibly.

title: How can RSEs stop researchers from re-inventing small programs instead of collaborating to sustain and improve big ones?
reasoning: This talk discusses RSE practices and how to encourage collaboration over reinvention across research teams, framed as a profession-wide issue using Katz's curve. While astrophysics is used as an example, the core message is about RSE practices and community/collaboration patterns.
abstract: Does it ever feel like lots of new research software in a particular domain is being released only to provide yet another way of performing an existing task, while researchers keep relying on decades-old packages for larger tasks (e.g. simulations)?  I'll introduce Daniel Katz's "software development curve" and use it to offer an explanation of why this happens.  I'll also show how this has played out recently in some areas of astrophysics and highlight where, and why, there have been notable exceptions.  Finally, I'll offer some ideas on how research software engineers can help research teams shift effort from independently re-inventing small programs to collaborating more effectively and widely on small, large, old or new research software.

title: What is new in Research Software Engineering in Germany?
reasoning: This talk is about the German RSE community, its development, policies, professional societies, and community-building initiatives — clearly about people and the profession.
abstract: In February 2023, the German RSE community came together at the deRSE23 conference in Paderborn in-person, for the first time since the global coronavirus pandemic. While this conference may represent the most visible marker of RSE activity in Germany, there are many more activities that show the progress that the German community has made over the last few years. This includes new developments in funding guidelines and policy, community building and infrastructures, collaborations, projects and research topics. In this talk, we will provide an update on the current status of research software in Germany and some of the most interesting developments, not only to share our successes, but also to identify remaining challenges and initiate further knowledge exchange across borders. The talk is informed by relevant initiatives in Germany, such as the German Society for Research Software - de-RSE, as well as their collaboration with other professional societies. It features developments and RSE activities from the Helmholtz Association of German Research Centers and universities, as well as the German National Research Data Infrastructure (NFDI), and further relevant initiatives. We will furthermore look at topics emerging in Germany with regard to research on research software itself. The talk finally focuses on the development of the RSE community in Germany itself, and serves as invitation to take part in upcoming activities, such as the second Germany-wide RSE event in 2023: the de-RSE unconference.

title: Evaluation of solutions for data-driven health research networks
reasoning: This talk evaluates data federation solutions specifically for healthcare/health research networks in Scotland, making it domain-specific to health research.
abstract:
Health data research is challenging because of the different data challenges e.g. governance, security, federation, lack of standardisation, historically poor infrastructure etc. The implementation of the secondary use of healthcare data in Scotland is fragmented, with data providers/processors using different query languages, data storage models and standards of various kinds (e.g. coding, vocabulary). To unite data from geographically decentralised databases, data federation solutions interconnect multiple databases and make data operations interoperable between data controllers/processors can improve efficiency and transparency of how data are used (through more unified processes) thus gaining more confidence from the general public.
Several initiatives/software solutions have been launched over the last decade or so to support access to healthcare data. This work will characterise the existing national and international data-driven health research networks and their software solutions from a methodological, technical and organisational perspective, to meet the needs of the Scottish Safe Haven Network. Our characterisation is based on a framework (compose with principles, architecture and model) that is inspired by the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) layer model. Existing federation solutions from proprietary and open-source platforms are reviewed and systematically assessed. The work intends to show the functionalities and responsibilities of all the participating partners. Different modes of operations (cohort discovery, distributed analysis and data extraction) are considered and discussed through the framework.

title: A Global Revolt: Incrementally Refactoring Global State Out of a Legacy Codebase
reasoning: This is about a general software engineering technique (refactoring global state, incremental testing) applicable across codebases, not tied to a specific research domain.
abstract:
To create and sustain a culture of open science in computational fields it is not enough simply to open source your software; your codebase must also be approachable, robust, and maintainable. This requires a codebase that is clearly documented, thoroughly tested, and above all well-designed. While researchers are beginning to understand this need for new software, there are many legacy codebases which have been written in a "write-only" style. 

One of the most common ways this presents itself is through an over-reliance on global state. This leads to many connected issues such as increased on-boarding time for new developers, difficulty testing the code effectively, and higher risk when making changes to the code. However, removing pervasive global state is a complex and time-consuming process, and attempting to do so in one go can make it harder to trust the changes and hinder progress in other areas of development. 

In this talk we present an incremental approach that we took to reduce our codebase's reliance on global state, without halting other ongoing work. In particular, we present a strategy for introducing unit-testing to legacy code, bypassing the need for the large amounts of mocking required if the global-state issue is unaddressed. We discuss the tools we used to help us, as well as the difficulties we faced and the lessons we learnt. The talk also offers guidance for adopting this approach in your own work, allowing you to create a codebase that fully embraces open science.

title: Pre-Processing Android Application PacKages (APKs) for Static Analysis at Scale - A lesson learned from developing AppInspect
reasoning: AppInspect is a research tool specifically for studying Android apps - a domain-specific research application. The talk centers on a tool built for a particular research need (Android app analysis for non-technical researchers).
abstract:
This talk will share a lesson learned from the development of AppInspect - a research tool enabling non-technical researchers to study Android apps.  The talk will focus on AppInspect's technique of pre-processing Android PacKage (APKs) for static analysis at scale.  The pre-processing enables the mining of thousands of Android apps for the reuse of code and resources, questionable system calls, suspicious libraries and their evolution.
An APK file is essentially a ZIP archive that contains a collection of files.  An Android app is a set of files of different elements, such as code, icons, images, and user interfaces.  Extracting elements from an APK using existing tools creates a deep hierarchy of directory structure.  The overhead of file lookup in a directory is costly, and the I/O performance of most file systems decreases as the number of files increases.  The use of existing tools alone to work with a large number of APKs would be very inefficient and take a long time to run an analysis.
The author finds that pre-processing the files within an APK is key to enabling the efficient processing of researchers' queries.  AppInspect transforms the diverse files within an APK into a tabular format based on Apache Parquet, which is optimised for storing a huge amount of data for the purpose of analysis.  A key advantage of the technique is compatibility with major big data analytics tools, support of different data types, and optimised for use in distributed computing infrastructure.

title: RSE specialisation: Research Computing Engineer

abstract: In this talk, we will discuss the research software engineering specialisation, particularly the role of Research Computing Engineers (RCEs) at the Alan Turing Institute. The discussion will cover the establishment of the Research Computing team, the types of projects and services RCEs provide, and the unique set of skills required for this position compared to more traditional Research Software Engineer positions. Through examples of projects, we will demonstrate how RCEs work with AI researchers to provide digital infrastructure and support for their research. We will also delve into capturing the emerging needs and current blockers of using national/regional supercomputers and public cloud platforms by the AI community at the Alan Turing Institute and beyond.

title: Quickly Building Operational Research Tools with a User-Friendly GUI Using Free Cloud-Hosted Jupyter Notebook: A Case Study of TikTok Video Analysis
reasoning: The talk centers on a general-purpose technique—using free cloud-hosted Jupyter Notebooks to rapidly build user-friendly GUI tools for non-technical researchers. While the case study involves TikTok video analysis, the core message is cross-cutting tooling methodology applicable across domains.
abstract:
The poster will illustrate the story of building the research tool "Video Frame and Audio Extractor" in a week based on a free cloud-based Jupyter Notebook, and making the tool user-friendly for non-technical researchers studying TikTok videos.    
One of the authors initially faced challenges in extracting frames from a large number of videos using ffmpeg's command-line interface, which was hardly usable by researchers without technical expertise.   The challenge hampers non-technical researchers' agency in studying TikTok videos.  
In preparation for a workshop on studying TikTok videos at Digital Methods Winter School 2023, the authors used a freely available cloud-hosted Jupyter Notebook to build a tool with a graphical user interface that invokes ffmpeg to extract frames from videos.   The tool was built, tested and made operational within a week.   Participants in the workshop, who are mostly without technical backgrounds, found the new tool easy to use, and their agency in researching TikTok videos increased.  
The poster discusses the design of the "Video Frame and Audio Extractor" tool and highlights the potential of using free cloud-hosted Jupyter Notebooks for building operational research tools with a graphical user interface quickly.
