title: Is Research Software Engineering in Computer Science different? The role of Artifact Evaluation
reasoning: This talk discusses the nature of RSE work within Computer Science as a discipline and the artifact evaluation process as a recognition/quality mechanism for research software. It's about the profession and cross-disciplinary practices rather than a specific tool or domain research.
abstract:
Many of the applications developed by research software engineers are for disciplines that do not conduct research into computation, for example, biology and chemistry. Is the research software engineering that takes place with a computation-focussed discipline like Computer Science different?
To begin answering this question, I will start from my own experiences as a researcher who develops software in a research programming language. Over the last few years I have become aware of the role of RSEs, as well as understanding the aspects of my own role that are research software engineering. I will also talk more broadly about software development within Computer Science research.
In particular, I will talk about the use of a process called artifact evaluation that has been adopted by a number of sub-disciplines of Computer Science. This process has been around for about a decade and evaluates the research software associated with conference and journal publications. Two of my papers have artifact evaluation badges and I will describe the process and how it relates to similar processes outside Computer Science.

title: Standardising UK Trusted Research Environments in the Open
reasoning: SATRE is a cross-cutting reference specification/standard for trusted research environments applicable across domains, with heavy emphasis on community engagement and multi-institution collaboration. The infrastructure/standard itself is general-purpose (Software), but a major focus is community building and stakeholder engagement.
abstract:
SATRE — Standardised Architecture for Trusted Research Environments — is a multi-institutional project developing and implementing a reference specification for trusted research environments (TREs) using an open, collaborative approach.
Personal or sensitive data which has been collected for operational, commercial or governmental reasons need to be managed securely and safely in a trusted environment that encourages best practice. However, most TREs are developed independently by siloed teams, resulting in TREs that are incompatible with each other, and aren’t conducive to collaborative research.
By making a standardised reference specification openly available, the SATRE team is working to break down these siloes and facilitate ground-breaking research with sensitive data across domains and industries.
A standard approach can work only if it has widespread support. The specification is openly developed through an extensive stakeholder engagement plan that goes beyond technically minded operators and developers, and includes the general public as well as high-level commissioners. Setting up open collaborative spaces, and actively reaching out to the community and the public, is critical for the success and sustainability of the project.
As we approach the end of our funding window, we will present our achievements and progress, including: 
Building and formalising the specification with multi-stakeholder input
Developing standards in the open
Achieving community engagement and consensus
Managing cross-institution collaborations
Ensuring the continuation of engagement and contribution beyond the project
We will also highlight how the RSE community can continue to contribute to the project and influence the future of how sensitive data are used with TREs!

title: Carpentries Offline: Running a Carpentries Workshop without the Internet
reasoning: CarpentriesOffline is a tool/platform supporting Carpentries training delivery. The artifact itself is software (a deployable system), but its purpose is community training/curriculum delivery. It's cross-cutting (not domain-specific) and serves the RSE/training community.

CarpentriesOffline (https://carpentriesoffline.org) is an out of the box solution for running a Carpentries workshop from a single device such as a Raspberry Pi, old laptop or even a dedicated server. This poster will describe:
The architecture of the CarpentriesOffline system
The build process that automates the creation of OS images in GitHub Actions
Ways to download and deploy it yourself
How to get involved with the project

title: Scottish Medical Imaging (SMI) – providing safe and secure access to research-ready, population scale health and imaging data
reasoning: This is about a domain-specific platform (medical imaging research environment) built for healthcare research, requiring discussion of the medical/health domain to explain.
abstract:
Routinely collected text-based health care records and associated imaging data are extremely useful for healthcare research. However, using such data is challenging and requires specialist tools and skills to work with. Trusted Research Environments (TREs) such as Scottish Medical Imaging (SMI) provide the capabilities and controls needed to unlock the value of such data whilst ensuring patient confidentiality.
We share our solutions to some of the major research challenges faced in establishing SMI and making imaging data research-ready, through the PICTURES collaboration:
Cataloguing – the metadata that describes each image, series or study is often inconsistent, incomplete or incorrect, making it very difficult to reliably index and catalogue image data for cohort building.
Natural Language Processing – useful image descriptors can be found in associated Radiology Reports, specifically free-text notes describing expert observations and diagnosis.
Pixel anonymisation – many scanning devices or secondary processing steps result in Personally Identifiable Information (PII) being burnt-in to the images themselves, requiring tools and methods for identifying and removing PII from pixel data at-scale.
This poster will cover the work of the PICTURES programme to enhance Trusted Research Environments to support AI development on large scale data, whilst protecting patient confidentiality. The SMI Service will be presented, which can support researchers and industry partners to train new models on routinely collected imaging data linked to healthcare records from the whole Scottish Population.

title: What is the evidence for Agile software development methodologies and their practices?
reasoning: This talk examines evidence for Agile methodologies and practices in software development, a cross-cutting software engineering practice topic relevant to RSEs broadly, not tied to a specific research domain.
abstract:
It's common practice for an RSE project to follow an Agile software development methodology or at least a process which is inspired by it. But how much evidence is there for the different methodologies (e.g. Scrum, XP, Lean) and their practices (e.g. pair-programming)?

Measuring the success of a project and productivity of a team is difficult, and we know that teams can vary widely in how well they adopt a set of practices. In light of this, researchers have attempted to account for this by using surrogate measures, case-studies, interviews and surveys. I'll explore the levels of evidence for these techniques and their tradeoffs. This talk will have some interactive voting to see how your intuition matches with the research so have your phones or laptops at the ready.

By the end of the talk attendees should understand what factors affect the effectiveness of different practices and have some references to help make the case for using them.

title: Natural Language Processing of Radiology Reports
reasoning: This is about NLP tools built specifically for medical/radiology reports in a healthcare research archive — domain-specific application.
abstract:
The Scottish Medical Imaging (SMI) archive holds a copy of Scotland’s radiology images for use by researchers. It includes radiology reports in text format for CT, MRI, Ultrasound, and other modalities. The PICTURES project has been funded to do research and development of tools and techniques for making the archive more easily accessible and usable. 
The natural language processing (NLP) work package has been doing research into methods for removing all Personally Identifiable Information (PII) from the free-text reports. The aim is to detect and remove names, dates, and other PII which may appear anywhere in the text. The process must be robust enough to give confidence that reports can be delivered to researchers without the risk of re-identifying patients. 
A second aim is to catalogue the text to make it easier to find reports about specific medical conditions, treatments or drugs. This labels the text using concepts defined in the UMLS metathesaurus, a comprehensive medical ontology, and it has the ability to spot different phrases with the same meaning. The medical reports are all associated with radiology images so this approach to building cohorts can be used to search the archive for relevant images as well as reports. 
This poster describes the work to build an acceptable NLP solution for detecting PII, the validation process, the design of a process for extracting medical concepts from reports and a database for cataloguing them, and a web service with cohort building tool plugin for querying the catalogue.

title: Cloud native approaches to environmental data processing and presentation
reasoning: While the projects are environmental/oceanographic, the talk's focus is on cross-cutting cloud-native data formats and object storage techniques (COG, Zarr, Kerchunk, Geoparquet) applicable broadly. However, the case studies are specific environmental domain projects.
abstract:
This talk will discuss the use of cloud native data formats in two projects. The first project, a virtual representation of an environmental system ( Environmental Digital Twin) presents several geospatial datasets relating to the Haig Fras Marine Conservation Zone. The second project processes global ocean circulation models, making them ready to be accessed by the public. 

Common to both projects are S3 like object stores run on STFC's JASMIN system. Object stores allow large datasets to be published without the need to run a dedicated web server. They store data in parallelised filesystems which can handle many simultaneous reads. In the case of JASMIN the object store is also co-located with high performance computing facilities which can process this data without moving it over the internet. Object stores support HTTP range requests allowing a partial download of an object. 
Both projects have used several cloud optimised file formats which rely on only transferring subsets of a file. This is especially useful for web applications where the user cannot practically transfer multi-gigabyte files.  
For geospatial raster data such as bathymetric maps and seabed images Cloud Optimised GeoTIFF format has been used. For vector data the Geoparquest, MBtiles and Flatgeobuf formats have been investigated. 
For the ocean circulation model output the Zarr and Kerchunk formats have been used. 
This talk will present some of the pros and cons of each of these file formats, the performance implications of using them, some of the issues encountered and how they were overcome.

title: Call to action! We need the RSE community’s help to protect sensitive personal data whilst also enabling secure scalable research: Trusted Research Environments (TREs) and Reproducible Research
reasoning: This talk is about Trusted Research Environments — secure data infrastructure that spans multiple domains (health, education, etc.) and is a cross-cutting platform/tooling concern. It calls on the RSE community to contribute, but the focus is on the software/infrastructure space rather than profession/career topics.
abstract: Across the country, data are collected for administrative purposes by a range of groups such as the health and social services, HMRC, education services and the police to answer key research questions which could not be answered without access to the data. Quite rightly, for ethical and legal reasons, these data must be handled securely thus protecting the confidentiality of the data subjects. Trusted Research Environments (TREs) (also known as Safe Havens or Secure Data Environments) are environments where researchers can assess de-identified data without being able to export the individual level data. TREs generally follow the Five Safes principles (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_safes) and are tightly controlled, with research users unable to access the internet during whilst in the TRE, and able to export only aggregate level information e.g. a graph or a table. Historically, as data from TREs cannot be shared, this often means that the technology innovations that have been made (such as infrastructure as code, software tools, data cleaning, curating, and analysis pipelines) have also not been shared and enhanced like they have in other disciplines. There is also a need for innovative research in federated solutions, data standards and reproducible research. The field needs the input of the RSE community to innovate in this space and bring ideas and solutions from other disciplines!

title: Firedrake: High productivity FEM simulations utilising sophisticated code generation
reasoning: Firedrake is a framework for solving PDEs via FEM — while it's used in scientific computing, it's a general-purpose computational tool applicable across many research domains (engineering, physics, etc.) rather than tied to one discipline. Code generation and HPC scaling are cross-cutting software techniques.
abstract:
Firedrake is a software framework providing an automated system for solving partial differential equation (PDEs) using the finite element method (FEM) and offers a better alternative to handwriting bespoke code for simulations. Using code generation, Firedrake provides mathematicians, scientists, and engineers with a very high productivity way to create high performance simulations. 
PDE-constrained optimisation and data assimilation problems can also be solved in Firedrake through the automatic differentiation framework: pyadjoint. 
Firedrake enables users to formulate PDEs using Unified Form Language (UFL), a Python based domain specific language. Using Firedrake's code generation layers produces fast and optimised C code to assemble finite element matrices, providing substantial advantages over the classical approach of manually coding entire simulations in C. This capability allows Firedrake users to rapidly prototype different mathematical formulations, discretisations, and solvers with ease. With seamless parallelism and sophisticated code generation prototyped solutions can then be scaled to thousands of cores on a High Performance Computer (HPC).
Workshop attendees will leave with an understanding of Firedrake's capabilities, including the advantages of code generation. We hope attendees will consider using Firedrake in their research or recommend it to their colleagues. 
Interested participants can view tutorial material (https://firedrakeproject.org/notebooks.html) ahead of time, but this is not a prerequisite.

title: Coding Confessions
reasoning: This is about normalising mistakes and knowledge sharing among RSEs as a profession—about people, culture, and community-building, not a specific tool or domain.
abstract:
What?
At "Coding Confessions" software developers talk openly about mistakes they've made when developing software.
Why?
People don’t want to talk about their mistakes, publish code or submit it for review. Common reasons for this are fears that “my code isn’t good enough”, “isn’t complete enough”, “has mistakes in it”. We want to encourage people to share their coding insecurities to help normalise talking about mistakes and knowledge gaps.

How?
We propose two parts to the event: 
1. A public panel where several (preferably senior) RSEs and software developers each take it in turn to talk openly about a mistake they've made in software they've developed. They will briefly describe the software system, the mistake they made and the they lessons learned from it. 
2. An anonymous form where attendees can disclose their confessions.  
Ultimately we will publish a collection of confessions as blog posts from both the panel and noticeboard on our website (https://coding-confessions.github.io/). This will help to highlight mistakes and stop them being repeated by others.

title: Mutation testing: Who tests the testers?
reasoning: This talk is about mutation testing as a general software testing technique, applicable across domains—a cross-cutting software engineering practice.
abstract:
Mutation testing is an advanced software testing technique. Imagine altering a '<' to '>' in your code; ideally, your unit tests should catch this. But do they? This walkthrough will explore the principles of mutation testing, demonstrating how it can uncover hidden weaknesses within supposedly robust test suites.
Using the third-party Python package Mutmut, I will illustrate common pitfalls in unit testing and show how mutation testing can expose these effectively. These examples will cover some simple examples and then go on some examples found in code bases. 
I will also show how mutation testing can be used as a teaching tool for better testing, including how it can highlight edge cases in unit tests.

title: Research Directions for Multi-Disciplinary RSE Research to Impact RSE Practise

abstract:
Check https://irser.github.io/ for updates.
With this panel, we intend to highlight the concept of RSE Research as a complementary approach to RSE Practise: conducting research to understand and improve how software is developed for research purposes. RSE Research should be a multi-disciplinary endeavour, involving disciplines such as software engineering, sociology, economics, and psychology, among others.
The overarching aim of research software engineering is to support and advance research fields by providing high-quality software that is reliable, efficient, and user-friendly. A distinctive aspect of RSE is that requirements are often not predetermined but emerge and evolve as research progresses. Understanding these requirements can be challenging without expertise in the relevant scientific field. Verification and validation are complex and adhere strictly to scientific standards.
RSE Research seeks to enhance the understanding of research software development and to devise methods, techniques, and tools to improve RSE Practise. Consequently, RSE Research addresses a range of research questions, which encompass not only the software as a product but also the provision of software development support for domain researchers, recognising their limited time and potentially improvable software development skills.
The objective of this panel is to explore the potential impact of RSE Research on RSE Practise, and the consequently emerging questions for RSE Research.
Panellists: Wilhelm Hasselbring (chair, Kiel University & University of Southampton), Michelle Barker (Research Software Alliance, Australia), Neil Chue Hong (University of Edinburgh), Simon Hettrick (University of Southampton), Inga Ulusoy (University of Heidelberg).

title: PlasmaFAIR: Improving the Sustainability of Software in Plasma Science
reasoning: PlasmaFAIR is a domain-specific support project for plasma science researchers, providing software engineering support to plasma physics codes like Pyrokinetics and Scotty. abstract:
The PlasmaFAIR project provides free software support to researchers at all career stages within the plasma science community. Our ethos is centred on the FAIR principles[1], which state that data and software should be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable. We aim to improve the ease-of-use, robustness and sustainability of plasma software by reviewing projects and making recommendations via our software ‘health checks’ and by working alongside scientists to provide direct software engineering support.
Our projects often include the addition of testing and documentation frameworks, the implementation of automation techniques, and the packaging of software for wider distribution. We also provide longer-term support for some projects. One example is Pyrokinetics[2], which acts as a translation layer between multiple plasma physics simulation codes to enable easier cross-code comparisons and parameter scans. Following work to redesign and simplify some of its core procedures, Pyrokinetics has rapidly become a community tool supported across multiple institutions. Similarly, our work on Scotty[3], a synthetic diagnostic for plasma experiments developed as a PhD project at the University of York and the Culham Centre for Fusion Energy, has resulted in fully-fledged research software with an international user base spanning from Singapore to San Diego.
Beyond our work supporting plasma physics software projects, we also contribute to open-source community tools such as netCDF and FAIRDataPipeline[4], and we develop new tools where the need arises.
More information is available at https://plasmafair.github.io.

CodeRefinery is a project teaching FAIR research software and development and basic Research Software Engineering practices to students and researchers across all research fields. CodeRefinery is a collaboration between universities and organizations in the Nordics funded by Nordic e-infrastructure collaboration (NeiC).
Our workshops are streamed and recorded so that anyone can follow them. Registered participants also have the possibility to interact with the instructors on stream via a collaborative document. The open source materials (available at https://coderefinery.org/lessons/) include lectures as well as hands-on activities. Sharing reusable training materials is one of the projects core values.
CodeRefinery works with local partners to facilitate an interactive and collaborative workshop despite the challenges of large audiences and online teaching. The local partner provides an online or in-person room with a team-lead. The participants watch the stream together and discuss and work on exercises in the group under guidance of the team lead.This approach enables local partners to provide participants with a full workshop while maintaining the benefits of discussing and working together as a group.
This contribution will describe a workshop setup for scaling an interactive workshop to a few hundred participants while still keeping the interaction and community experience of a local small workshop. We kindly invite YOU to join our next workshop as a learner, team-lead or local partner.

title: Modern, interactive and impactful software documentation with Sphinx, MyST and the Diátaxis framework

abstract:
Software documentation is often perceived as important by developers, yet insufficiently written or maintained over time [1]. Although it is accepted that good documentation is essential to both users and developers of research software, it is challenged by insufficient training, periodic staff turnover and minimal resources dedicated to knowledge sharing [2]. In this context, the Diátaxis framework [3] offers a valuable proposition for achieving an optimal and quality design for software documentation.

This talk provides a practical introduction to the Diátaxis framework, using the Sphinx documentation tool coupled with the MyST ecosystem. The core principles behind the framework are first explained, followed by their application using Sphinx and MyST to produce quality materials, such as tutorials, cookbooks, user guides or developer references. The talk ends with some tips to automate and publish documentation alongside research code.

[2]: https://doi.org/10.1038/467775a

title: Boring Boilerplate Code Can Connect Communities: Lessons From the Astrophysics Code SNEWPY
reasoning: This talk centers on a specific astrophysics code (SNEWPY) built for nuclear/particle astrophysics communities, making it domain-specific Research, though it has strong Community/collaboration themes.
abstract:
We’re not usually excited about writing boilerplate code. It’s boring. It’s a chore. However, when used well, boilerplate code can have a dramatic impact.
In this talk, I will introduce the astrophysics code SNEWPY. By providing all the boilerplate code necessary to combine work by nuclear astrophysicists, theoretical particle physicists and experimental particle physicists, SNEWPY has enabled closer collaboration and dramatically reduced the time necessary to generate physics results. SNEWPY was also incorporated as a dependency into multiple third-party codes, making them more versatile while avoiding duplication of effort and reducing the risk of bugs.
I will illustrate how writing code that is FAIR, maintainable, reproducible and accessible has connected these communities and improved physics research outcomes.

title: Re-runnable code is all you need
reasoning: This talk focuses on Devbox, a general-purpose tool for reproducible computing environments applicable across research domains, making it a cross-cutting software/reproducibility tooling topic.
abstract: Reproducibility is fundamental to scientific integrity but is increasingly compromised by the common practices of publishing papers without code, or sharing code that cannot be executed easily on another computer due to unmanaged dependencies and computing environments. This talk introduces the landscape of tools that enable researchers to overcome these barriers, with a focus on Devbox, a tool designed to encapsulate computing environments. With Devbox it is easy to ensure that scientific code is not just runnable but also replicable across various systems. By highlighting specific case studies, this session demonstrates how Devbox and similar technologies can transform research workflows, dramatically saving time with automation, making it easier to collaborate, and enhancing the credibility of results. Attendees will gain actionable strategies to implement a culture of reproducibility, making their research transparent and reproducible with minimal effort.

title: A gentle guide to using the {targets} package for analytic pipelines
reasoning: The talk is about using the {targets} R package as a general pipeline tool for analytic workflows—a cross-cutting reproducibility/software practice applicable across domains.
abstract:
Data analysis is an iterative process. Data cleaning, exploratory data analysis (EDA), and model fitting are rarely run without a hitch from start to finish. Each step takes time, and often requires revisiting earlier steps to correct for newly discovered problems. For example, in performing EDA, you can unearth a text issue that requires revisiting data cleaning. When you are finally done with the analysis, you will need to reproduce it to check it all works as expected.

To reproduce the analysis, there is a temptation to run the code again from the top, which may take a long time. You can save time by saving model outputs, but if you make a change to an earlier data cleaning step, you’ll need to update everything that depends on that. You can write code to manage these dependencies, but this is a hard problem. Fortunately, “pipeline tools” are an existing approach to manage these dependencies. They take care of the details of watching which files and relevant code changes, and only run the necessary parts. The {targets} R package is one popular pipeline approach, providing extensive documentation and user support. However, it presents a different coding practice that might not be familiar.  

In this interactive walkthrough, I will gently introduce the ideas behind {targets}, and will live code a data analysis using {targets} from scratch, warts and all. I encourage questions throughout the live coding walkthrough, so you can understand the process and see how this could benefit your own work.

title: The HPC and RSE Experience Programme
reasoning: This is about a career pathway/training programme for RSEs, focused on people and professional development.
abstract: The Imperial College Research Computing Service is running a programme that will create a pathway into RSE and HPC careers. This program is called the HPC and RSE Experience Programme and is a six month job for Early Career Researchers wanting to dip their toes in the world of HPC and RSE. This program gives them exposure to working as an RSE and working alongside the HPC sys admins and user support staff. We are enthusiastic about this programme, it is a great training and career development opportunity for the participants and it expands the pool of RSE and HPC-aware researchers in the wider community. We have run three iterations of this and the fourth one will be starting a couple of months after RSECon24. We would like to use this poster as an opportunity to discuss ideas with the community to improve the structure of the programme and encourage other RSE groups to run similar programmes.

title: Impact of Using A Modern Compiler and Optimized Workflow on the Performance of a Complex Nuclear Fusion Application for ITER
reasoning: This talk centers on optimizing PARTICLE-3D, a nuclear fusion application for ITER, making it domain-specific research software, though it offers generalizable optimization methodology.
abstract:
Harnessing the vast computational power of HPC systems empowers us to expedite and magnify our efforts, effectively addressing intricate challenges spanning various domains. Yet, optimizing scientific applications to fully exploit this potential necessitates substantial expertise and dedication to code optimization.
This work presents a pragmatic approach tailored to enhance the performance of PARTICLE-3D (P3D), a nuclear fusion application code crucial for simulating runaway electron dynamics—a critical aspect impacting the operational lifespan of nuclear fusion machines like ITER. Transitioning from a legacy compiler dependency, the authors identified performance bottlenecks within the serial version of the code, particularly pertaining to I/O communication between subroutine calls. By meticulously restructuring the code and refining inter-subroutine communication, the article highlights the process adopted by the authors to unlock embarrassingly parallel computation workflow on the HPC cluster. The optimized version of P3D exhibits a performance improvement of several orders of magnitude compared to its base version. These optimizations not only elevated the performance but also improved the code portability, ensuring seamless integration with diverse HPC architectures equipped with modern compilers. 
The methodology described here can serve as a valuable case study for early researchers and code developers to enhance the performance of any such code designed for problems characterised by the similar algorithmic topologies.

title: Performant Python Patterns: Small changes to speed up your Python code
reasoning: General-purpose Python performance techniques applicable across domains; cross-cutting software engineering practice.
abstract:
Python is a highly accessible programming language commonly used by researchers, most of whom are not formally trained programmers. It’s easy to get software working with Python, and equally as easy to overlook the requirements for your Python code to be performant.

This interactive talk presents multiple versions of common Python programming patterns, attendees will have the opportunity to vote (via Wooclap) for which they think is fastest or the expected speedup, before the answer is displayed and explained.

Writing performant code is often overlooked but can increase research productivity, improve shared resource availability (e.g. HPC) and reduce energy usage. This talk aims to expose how some small changes to Python code, and using packages such as NumPy and pandas correctly, can lead to big performance improvements.

title: Developing PyCam: Software for acquiring and processing volcanic UV SO2 camera data
reasoning: PyCam is software purpose-built for volcanology (SO2 monitoring in volcanic plumes), a specific research domain. Cannot describe without naming the discipline.
abstract:
Monitoring of sulphur dioxide (SO2) emission rates in volcanic plumes provides valuable insights into the state of a volcanic system, aiding eruption forecasting efforts for many volcanoes worldwide. SO2 cameras exploit the strong absorption signature of SO2 at ultraviolet (UV) wavelengths to measure emission rates with UV-sensitive cameras. However, this approach has been limited by the cost of traditional scientific-grade equipment. In 2016 a group from The University of Sheffield developed PiCam UV, an imaging system based on a low-cost modified visible imaging detector that produces comparable data to traditional equipment at a fraction of the cost.

Whilst previous work has developed open-source libraries for processing SO2 camera data, the software has been complex and incredibly difficult for end users to utilise. Development of the PyCam software began in mid-2019 to provide a user-friendly, graphical interface for interacting with PiCam systems, i.e. remotely adjusting settings and on- and off-line processing of collected data. RSE involvement began in early 2023 and will continue until at least 2025, with the aim of improving the quality, sustainability and usability of the software going forward. This is of particular importance to this project since the end users may not be experts in remote sensing or programming, but need to generate reliable SO2 emission rates to combine with other strands of volcano monitoring data (e.g. seismics).

Here, we give a brief overview of the PiCam hardware and PyCam software, describe the work already completed to improve PyCam, and outline the future work planned.

title: Reproducible distributed research in practice
reasoning: This describes a general-purpose tool ('orderly') for reproducible research workflows and data provenance, applicable across research domains rather than tied to a specific discipline.
abstract:
Have you ever tried version-controlling a data set with git and then using code from the same git repository to track it? Or tried to track different versions of outputs from one analysis as you use them in another? Or shared and collaborated on those analyses outputs as you might share code, docker containers or virtual machines? If so, you have probably run into limitations of our current tooling, just like all the other researchers who hit these problems every day.
In this talk we show how a multilingual distributed analysis approach we developed enables researchers to stop thinking about the details and facilitates collaboration and reproducibility.  Our approach ("orderly") tries to address shortcomings in existing data-versioning and workflow tools to enable researchers to automatically track provenance in data and analysis products as they move from output of one analysis to inputs in another. Our tool is neither a workflow or data-versioning tool that forces data to behave like code. Instead, it leans on metaphors from containerisation by allowing researchers to compose together analyses from building blocks of previous analyses which expose a simple interface describing their inputs and outputs.  Our system is designed to be progressive, scaling from a single user on a laptop to a distributed collection of researchers sharing "packets" of data via a web application.
The world probably does not need more workflow tools, but our experience indicates there are important researcher needs in data management that are still poorly met.

title: Solving the right problems: Requirements capture for large-scale, evolving research software
reasoning: This talk is about a domain-specific research software (OpenScan) for clinical trial/medical device data, focused on its redesign and requirements capture. The methodology (requirements capture) is general, but the subject is a specific health-research tool.
abstract:
A key challenge in designing sustainable research software is evaluating and meeting ongoing user needs. OpenScan is a National Institute for Health and Care Research Innovation Observatory (NIHRIO) project that collects, standardises, analyses, and publishes international clinical trial and medical device data. Since OpenScan's initial development, NIHRIO has faced challenges with maintaining, expanding, and fully utilising the project for their research, in part due to its complex technical stack and Amazon Web Services (AWS) infrastructure. 
NIHRIO enlisted the Newcastle University RSE Team to update and re-design components of OpenScan to address these issues. We began by evaluating and documenting the design, including how NIHRIO currently uses OpenScan. We then captured the long-term requirements of NIHRIO's developers and researchers. This process highlighted that, in addition to NIHRIO's stated requirements, we needed to address challenges with account management, documentation, and reproducible workflows.
In this talk, we discuss capturing OpenScan2's requirements using interviews, user stories, and work packages. We highlight one of the workflow challenges that we uncovered: updating the web scrapers that collect OpenScan's data. Finally, we show how we designed new solutions to address these barriers.
OpenScan's redesign demonstrates the importance of requirements capture when developing and (re-)designing research software. Ultimately, ensuring we solve the right problems will help make OpenScan a sustainable resource that enables innovative research on medical progress.

title: OpenGHG - A community platform for greenhouse gas data analysis
reasoning: OpenGHG is a domain-specific platform built for greenhouse gas research, clearly tied to atmospheric/climate science.
abstract:
To address the urgent need to understand changes in greenhouse gas (GHG)  emissions, there has been dramatic growth in GHG measurement and modelling systems in recent years. This growth has led to substantial challenges; to date, there has been little standardisation of data products, and the interpretation of GHG data requires combined information from numerous models.
    OpenGHG is a platform that offers data retrieval from various public archives, data standardisation, and researcher-friendly data analysis tools. It helps researchers overcome the challenges posed by independent networks,  archival standards, and varying spatial and temporal scales in greenhouse gas research. OpenGHG has an internal set of standards into which different data formats are converted. It offers data analysis and visualisation tools, a Jupyter Notebook interface, and will offer options for both cloud and local installations. Additionally, to handle large data we have employed the Zarr storage system for efficient file storage handling

    This presentation will demonstrate recent developments in OpenGHG and its use in the development of a prototype "operational"  emissions evaluation system for the UK, the Greenhouse Gas Emissions  Measurement and Modelling Advancement (GEMMA). This system will combine bottom-up (inventory-based) and top-down (observation-based) approaches to evaluate emissions in near-real time.  An attempt will be made to shed light on some of the challenges faced and associated success stories that occurred during the development of this flexible and extensible community-led software to tackle scientific and technical challenges.

title: EVERSE: European Virtual Institute for Research Software Excellence
reasoning: EVERSE is a profession-wide, cross-organisation initiative establishing frameworks, networks, and recognition for research software quality across Europe — a community/policy infrastructure effort rather than a specific tool or domain research.
abstract:
EVERSE (European Virtual Institute for Research Software Excellence) is an EC-funded project that aims to establish a framework for research software excellence. The project brings together a consortium of European research institutions, universities, and infrastructure providers to collaboratively design and champion best practices for high-quality, sustainable research software. You can learn more about the project at https://everse.software/
The primary objective of EVERSE is to create a community-driven framework that empowers researchers and developers to produce, maintain, and share high-quality research software. The project will achieve this by consolidating existing best practices, developing the Research Software Quality Kit (RSQkit), integrating tools and services for software quality assessment, and engaging with the research community through pilots, training, and recognition initiatives.
EVERSE will establish a European network for research software quality, fostering collaboration among researchers, developers, and infrastructure providers. The project will actively engage with five European science clusters, ensuring that the developed framework is tailored to the specific needs of each scientific domain. These are: ENVRI-FAIR (environmental research), EOSC-Life (life sciences), ESCAPE (astronomy and particle physics), PaNOSC (photon and neutron sciences), and SSHOC (social sciences and humanities).
By championing research software quality and providing a supportive ecosystem for sustainable software development, EVERSE will contribute to the advancement of open science and reproducible research across various scientific domains. The project's outcomes will benefit researchers, research software engineers, and the broader scientific community, ultimately enhancing the quality, reliability, and impact of research software in Europe and beyond.

title: On the Tension between Agile Methodologies and Research Software
reasoning: This talk discusses agile software engineering practices as a cross-cutting methodology applicable to research software broadly, not tied to a specific domain. It also touches on profession/community aspects of how RSEs work.
abstract:
Over the last decades, software professionals have embraced agile development as the de-facto way of building software, but these practices have not seen widespread adoption in academia. In this talk, we will look at the reasons for this lack of adoption and how agile practices may be better adopted and adapted for the academic context.
Practices like pair programming, test-driven development, and daily standups are part of the toolkit of every software engineer in industry. However, the adoption of these practices in research contexts is limited. The research community recognises this issue, and there are multiple community efforts to improve engineering practices within research software, with initiatives like The Turing Way and The Carpentries.
Using our personal experiences –-both in industry and academia–- we will explain the unpopularity of agile in academia. We propose there is a tension between agile practices and the academic environment. For example, pair programming is incompatible with doctoral projects where a single student handles most of the coding; and daily standups are challenging with collaborators from different departments or universities.
We will discuss:
The range of agile practices available.
How industry and academic contexts differ.
How well different practices work in different contexts.
How agile practices might be adapted to various academic contexts.
We believe agile practices need to be translated to properly work in an academic context. In this talk, we describe our successful and unsuccessful attempts to develop academic-compatible agile practices, and discuss what we learned.

title: An introduction to Triplestores and the SPARQL Query Language for RSEs
reasoning: This is a tutorial introducing a general-purpose technology (triplestores and SPARQL) applicable across domains, fitting cross-cutting Software tooling. FAIR data is mentioned but the focus is on the technology itself.
abstract:
Triplestores are a form of graph database designed to store highly structured web-accessible data. They are widely used to store data that can be described in a consistent manner. The underlying data structure used in triplestores is also used to describe controlled vocabularies, such as DCAT - a vocabulary used to describe data catalogues. Knowledge of the structure of triplestores, and the related use of controlled vocabularies to describe datasets, increases an RSE's set of tools that can be used to publish, access, and understand data that that follows recognised standards. Triplestores and controlled vocabularies are key technologies in helping data become more Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR). 
This walkthrough will briefly introduce the technology stack generally used for hosting triplestores as well as the underlying data structure that is required to store data in a triplestore. I will then demonstate the power of the query language used for triplestores, SPARQL. I will exemplify the use of SPARQL via a range of SPARQL endpoints that exist in the wild across several subject domains, including the triplestore representation of the structured elements of Wikipedia, as well as scientific and geospatial examples providing access to large, diverse datasets. I will show some of the more advanced features of SPARQL, and how these compare with other APIs which may be more familiar to the audience. Finally, I will discuss the idea of federated querying, where a single query can be used to retrieve data from different databases distributed over a network.

title: Effortlessly creating Python packages with good practices.

abstract:
In this interactive session we will be creating a Python package from scratch. In order to create the package, the Python template developed by the Netherlands eScience Center (NLeSC) will be used (https://research-software-directory.org/software/nlesc-python-template). This template is used by the Research Software Engineers (RSE) of NLeSC and well adopted by the community of RSEs. The generated package will include the good practices used at the Netherlands eScience Center. Such generated package will have necessary components right at the start of the development process. Some of the features of the generated package are listed below.
Boilerplate unit tests and documentation
Python static analysis setup configuration
Open-source software license
Continuous integration with GitHub action workflows for building, testing, link checking and linting
Code style checking
Editor configuration
Usage and contribution documents:
documentation for package users
documentation for package developers
extensive documentation about project setup
Code of Conduct
Contributing guidelines
Continuous code quality and code coverage reporting using Sonarcloud
Automatic creation of issues with instructions how to pass all GitHub action workflows and integrate with services like Zenodo and Read the Docs
Instructions how to make package citable
FAIR software recommendation badge
Optional pre commit hook to catch lint errors early

title: Introducing Isambard-AI: new leadership-class UK facility to advance AI

This is a new leadership-class supercomputer funded by the Department of Science Innovation and Technology (DSIT) and UKRI to quickly address the lack of national AI-capable supercomputing facilities for open research. title: Automatic Assessment of Software Quality Indicators
reasoning: This talk is about KPIs/metrics for assessing research software quality in general — a cross-cutting software engineering practice applicable across domains. It also touches on profession-wide initiatives like FAIR/HERMES publication infrastructure.
abstract:
Software plays a vital role in research, but we do not know much about it's quality. There are no well defined indicators or even measurements, despite the software often being written by domain researchers with basic software engineering skills.
In this talk we want to introduce a set of key performance indicators (KPIs) provided by a working group of the German Helmholtz Association and present the results of a discussion we had in context of the HERMES project regarding them.
The goal of the suggested KPIs is to support assessment and evaluation of the quality of Research Software and datasets. While the set of indicators is not fixed yet, the working group already published a first draft of the metrics they are about to use at ArXiv. This involves an adopted maturity model (COBIT) with indicators for different dimensions.
The Hermes project regards KPIs as important metadata for the given artifacts, especially for Research Software. As Hermes is all about publication of software (and datasets) with rich, automatically collected metadata, it was our natural reaction to look into the planned indicators.

title: Discovering and bridging knowledge gaps between research software engineering and software engineering research
reasoning: This talk is about bridging two communities (RSEs and software engineering researchers), focusing on profession-wide collaboration and community-building rather than a specific tool or research domain.
abstract:
As RSEs, we apply software engineering methods, practices, and tools to research software. And despite the fact that - statistically - many of us haven’t had formal education in software engineering, we are the software experts in (academic) research in practice.
It's therefore astonishing that as a community, we haven’t traditionally had strong links, active communication, and frequent reciprocal collaborations with the other academic community that is concerned with software engineering methods, practices, and tools: software engineering researchers. Similarly, most software engineering researchers haven't studied research software and its community of developers, although both often are located in the SE researchers' own institutions. There is clearly a gap between our two communities, although it seems clear that we should be able to benefit from each other considerably: RSEs by having access to state-of-the-art software engineering knowledge, methods and tools, and software engineering researchers by gaining a whole new community of practice and their artifacts to investigate.
In this short presentation, we shine a light into the gap between the communities and on recent activities aiming to bring them closer together to unlock mutual benefits. We report on a Dagstuhl Seminar (https://www.dagstuhl.de/24161) where international representatives of the two communities met to understand each other better, find a common language, discover and identify knowledge gaps, and collaborate to build bridges that can potentially cross these gaps in both directions. We also present a common working group where a national RSE association and a national society for computer science come together to enable future collaboration.

title: Mining RSE repository timelines on GitHub: How long will it live, and who will notice?
reasoning: This is a research study analyzing RSE repository practices on GitHub - it's about understanding the RSE profession/community practices through data mining, producing insights about what makes research software repositories successful. It's meta-research about RSE practices.
abstract: Do your research software repositories have licenses? Do you use issues? Have you added contributing guidelines? And more importantly, does it make a difference? We mined ePrints publications and GitHub repositories to find out. We first scanned around 200,000 publications from UK universities for links to GitHub. Then, we manually identified links that pointed to software created for the publication to make sure that we were in fact looking at research software. Finally, we pulled a broad range of data about those repositories using the GitHub API and transformed those into a time-lined format. This allows us to analyse the lifecycle of a repository – when do potential users and contributors discover it, and when do they start engaging with the code, if at all? What aspects make or break the community’s engagement with your source code? Among other findings, our exploratory analysis suggests that leading by example encourages externals to submit issues and commits as well, and that repositories that manage to grow their contributor pool continue to increase their stars for longer. The resulting code base and data are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/softwaresaved/rse-repo-analysis).

title: Run-time data visualisation in C++ with morphologica
reasoning: morphologica is a general-purpose C++ visualization library applicable across domains, not tied to a specific research discipline. It's a cross-cutting tool for RSEs.
abstract:
As Research Software Engineers, we develop computer programs for scientific study. Often, a program describes a model of a system which may be used to make predictions or to test a hypothesis. These models may contain many state variables and the process of debugging and program verification can be aided by visualising the variables.

Sometimes, the best choice of programming platform for the model is a general purpose CPU with the program expressed in a compilable language such as C++. However, there is a limited selection of data visualisation libraries available for C++ and this can impede the development process.

morphologica is a relatively new library for visualisation in C++ programs. Developed at the University of Sheffield, it uses modern, shader-based OpenGL techniques to draw 2D and 3D graphs and objects with minimal processing overhead. It achieves this in a header-only design which is easy to integrate into a C++ program.

Users of morphologica are not expected to learn OpenGL techniques directly; custom visualizations can be achieved by using graphics primitives or with only a basic knowledge of how a triangle mesh is created for GL rendering.

morphologica has been used in a number of published scientific studies and is also used by the Research and Development teams at Opteran Technologies to aid algorithm development.
This workshop will guide participants through the process of incorporating morphologica data visualisation into their own C++ programs.

title: Scaling up computational reproducibility practices in research organisations - how to influence change
reasoning: This talk is about a framework for scaling reproducibility practices across research organisations, focused on organisational change, leadership, and profession-wide initiatives rather than a specific tool or domain.
abstract:
Attendees will learn how to use a framework created to assist research organisations in understanding how reproducibility (including computational reproducibility) can be scaled up internally. The framework can be used by a range of internal stakeholders with differing goals, such as institutional leaders seeking to align organisational strategies, or managers wishing to provide the support that staff in their part of the organisation may be seeking. 

The framework is a part of a report on how the practice of conducting research in a reproducible way can be scaled up from pioneers to the majority of researchers and research support staff.  Attendees will be introduced to the types of practices that assist individual researchers, research support staff, and managers to scale up practices that improve research reproducibility. Note that this framework is focused on how well organised an organisation is at scaling up reproducibility practices (i.e., access and coordination), not the maturity of reproducibility practices and how well they adhere to what is commonly understood to be best practice in reproducibility. The framework can be used to assess current practice, and facilitate discussion about priorities and directions. 

This report was commissioned by Knowledge Exchange, a group of national organisations from six European countries supporting research infrastructure and services to enable the use of digital technologies to improve higher education and research: CSC in Finland, CNRS in France, DeiC in Denmark, DFG in Germany, Jisc in the UK and SURF in the Netherlands.

title: A Data Downpour: Extending long-term UK climatological rainfall series by blending rescued historic data with current station sources.
reasoning: This talk centers on building software for a specific domain (UK climatology/rainfall data), blending historic rescued data with current sources to advance climate research. It's domain-specific research software.
abstract:
The Rainfall Rescue project was a remarkable effort to digitise historic UK monthly rainfall data. After scanning 66,000 pages of journals and weather logs dating back to the 17th century, the project, with the help of over 16,000 volunteers, transcribed 5.2 million observations stored in the Met Office National Meteorological Archive. This effort brought a wealth of historic data back to life.
Considering this newly recovered data, our project set out to create a comprehensive, fully traceable, blended monthly rainfall series for the UK that merged Rainfall Rescue with other primary sources, including MIDAS open (Met Office Integrated Data Archive System), which contains a large publicly available collection of UK mainland surface observations.
A key challenge when blending data sources is to avoid duplication. To tackle this, we developed efficient software to match combinations of gauge locations, station names and accumulated values. Once matched with certain criteria, we were able to extend back records of existing sites in our primary database, incorporating new data whilst preventing double counting.
As a Scientific Software Engineer (the Met Office equivalent of an RSE), I will present an overview of techniques and tooling we applied for this task, following the Research Software Development Principles to deliver maintainable and reproducible software. I will outline the methodologies and challenges of this work and emphasise steps we took to allow traceability and configurability. The preliminary results from this project have extended records for numerous sites, offering a richer monthly rainfall series to advance climate monitoring and research.

title: Demystifying Large Language Models
reasoning: This is an educational talk explaining how LLMs work conceptually—a cross-cutting AI topic relevant to RSEs broadly, not tied to a specific research domain or specific tool.
abstract:
Large language models (LLMs) have taken the world by storm over the past year or two, sparking a huge number of LLM-powered tools, products and start-ups. However, despite being readily accessible to us all, how these models work remains a mystery to many of us.
This talk will demysitify LLMs by providing an intuitive understanding of how they build upon key prior advances to successfully cross the uncanny valley of text generation, and provide an overview of the surprising range of other tasks mastering this "one weird trick" seems to let these models perform.
Participants will gain an intuition of how LLMs work by immersive participation in a human-powered "large audience model", as well as the opportunity to pit the latest LLMs against our very own RSECon Turing test.
This talk will provide participants with a conceptual understanding of how LLMs work, the history of prior advances that made them possible, and what makes these models "foundational". It will also explore some of the strengths and limitations of these models, including examples of where they do surpisingly well and where they can struggle with suprisingly similar tasks.
This talk won't make you an expert on word embeddings, deep neural networks or transformers, but it will give you a peek behind the curtain of how these seemingly magical models work and hopefully give you some tools to explain them to friends and family in an intuitive way.

title: Towards adoption of FAIR4RS: equipping researchers with FAIR research software skills

abstract:
Recently there has been growing recognition that research software, defined as “source code files, algorithms, scripts, computational workflows and executables that were created during the research process or for a research purpose”[1], should adhere to the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable) principles[2], as well as meeting broader open research goals such as reproducibility. A set of FAIR guidelines for research software (FAIR4RS) has been developed to provide a framework for the development of FAIR research software[1]. However, many researchers require additional practical support to meet these guidelines. Training is one aspect of cultural change needed to promote uptake of the FAIR4RS principles[3].

During this panel discussion we will consider the challenges involved in equipping researchers with the skills needed to create FAIR research software: what topics need to be covered, how can we reach our target audience, how can we fund these activities and how can we motivate trainees to carry forward the FAIR4RS principles?

This panel will benefit members of the community who are involved in training researchers in better research software practices or who work in settings where research outputs include software. We invite attendees to share their experiences and pool ideas for future provision of FAIR4RS training within the RSE community.

[1] Barker et al., 2022, ‘Introducing the FAIR Principles for Research Software’.
[2] Wilkinson et al., 2016, ‘The FAIR Guiding Principles for Scientific Data Management and Stewardship’.
[3] Barker et al., 2024, ‘The FAIR for Research Software Principles after two years’.

title: Tracking the Carbon Cost of Optimization Algorithms: A case study
reasoning: FitBenchmarking is a cross-cutting tool for comparing optimization algorithms, and the talk focuses on adding a carbon emissions metric—a sustainability tooling concern that applies broadly across research domains.
abstract:
One of the biggest global challenges is tackling climate change and building a sustainable future. The IT sector is estimated to account for 2-6% of global carbon emissions and is set to rise as much as 20% by 2030. Whilst software on its own doesn’t emit CO2, understanding the cost of running it is important so that the way it is developed, and the way it is used, can be optimised for minimal carbon emissions. There are several carbon tracking tools available for estimating hardware electricity power consumption, allowing users and developers to quantify the carbon cost of running a program and identify areas for improvement.
FitBenchmarking (https://fitbenchmarking.github.io/) is an open source Python package that allows users to compare the performance of different optimization algorithms and their implementations across various fitting problems, through metrics such as runtime and accuracy. In this talk, I will outline how a new carbon emissions metric has been added to FitBenchmarking, some of the challenges faced along the way, and the insight that reporting emissions offers developers and users of fitting software.

abstract:
Weather and climate research is an exciting and important field, today and for the future. Research software engineers play a crucial part in building and maintaining the large simulation models at numerous institutions in the UK and worldwide, processing and analysing the ever growing observational and simulated datasets, and developing the future infrastructure to deliver impact from cutting edge research. While there are pockets who are working to enable knowledge exchange (e.g. the Met Office Academic Partnership (MOAP) Community of Practice for Research Software Engineers and Scientific Software Engineers), we are missing an open and inclusive community for everyone working or interested in this field. 
…Or are we?
This event is aimed at bringing together Climate and Weather RSEs to learn from one another, network to form lasting partnerships, and discuss whether and what we are missing as a community. Do we want to form a Special Interest Group under the RSE Society? Do we want regular meetings or seminars? Or do we just need signposting to existing ones? What are the next steps for our community?
We will have presentations from various groups and institutions in the field, a panel discussion, and facilitate opportunities for networking and knowledge exchange.

The community covers a range of RSE roles from development of research software to support of HPC facilities, providing support to researchers. Our objectives are to provide peer support across the RSE HPC community, share experience and best practice, foster an open, self-sustaining community and collaborate with other, associated communities and organisations.

The event is split into two sessions: technical and training/community, with a break in between where HPC service providers can display small posters with updates on their services. Each session starts with two short presentations for setting the scene, followed by a panel discussion. title: Environmental impact and social responsibility in large scale HPC services: ARCHER2 case study

While ARCHER2 is a specific HPC platform, the discussion centers on cross-cutting sustainability practices and community advocacy applicable across DRI.
abstract: A period of major change is coming up in the UK HPC landscape both in terms of the services that will be available and the focus on environmental impact and social responsibility of HPC services. In this presentation I will give an overview of ongoing work associated with the environmental sustainability and social responsibility of the UK National Supercomputing Service, ARCHER2. This will cover the understanding and quantification of emissions associated with a large-scale HPC installation, ideas for reuse of waste heat, and work to protect and improve the biodiversity associated with the ACF data centre. I will also set the quantitative emissions estimates for ARCHER2 in context by comparing to other sources of emissions. Understanding emission is the first step, to have a wider impact, HPC emissions data need be exposed to users of HPC systems. We will discuss approaches for this to allow researchers to make informed decisions on how they maximise the environmental efficiency of their HPC use. In addition to environmental impact, the presentation will touch on social responsibility aspects including staff wellbeing and wider outreach work. Although much of this work has been centred around ARCHER2, many of the lessons learned and approaches taken are applicable across Digital Research Infrastructure (DRI) more generally, and provide a useful guide to which areas of environmental impact and social responsibility are well understood and where more work is needed by the community.

title: Building an efficient Continuous Integration workflow on HPC systems

abstract:
Continuous Integration (CI) is a central cornerstone of modern software development practices, but its usage in High Performance Computing (HPC) contexts brings a set of challenges that are yet to be tackled fully across different libraries and computing centers.
We want to share our own path in the development of a modern HPC library, moving from a single development node to multiple nodes and onto SLURM-managed HPC systems. We will cover the following topic areas:
Container image generation and deployment
Rootless container execution and custom executors
Interaction with SLURM through a custom executor or ephemeral runners
Accounting and security model
Build performance profiling and optimization
Test performance and split build/test execution
What do we need from computing center operators?

title: Utilising the flexible simulation software REvoSim for advanced evolutionary and ecological modelling
reasoning: REvoSim is a domain-specific simulation tool for ecology and evolution, used here to study predation and species diversity—a specific research question in ecology.
abstract:
The study of ecological trends and the mechanisms which drive them are pivotal for advancing our understanding of biodiversity and ecosystem functions. While traditional field studies are invaluable, they often face limitations due to the complexity and scale of natural systems. Computational models, such as REvoSim, offer a versatile platform for simulating ecological interactions and evolutionary trajectories, with exceptional flexibility in parameter manipulation. This allows for the detailed modulation of environmental conditions, behaviours of the digital organisms, and their interactions. 
This poster aims to demonstrate how REvoSim can be utilised to replicate real-world ecological trends and delve into the driving forces behind these patterns. The research specifically explored the impact of predation on species diversity across varying levels of environmental heterogeneity. The results of the simulation supported empirical data produced in field studies and further investigation aimed to explain why this phenomena occurs. 
By highlighting the capabilities of this software, this poster aims to showcase REvoSim's potential as a powerful tool for ecological and evolutionary research, offering the ability to test hypotheses and predict outcomes in a controlled yet dynamic digital system.

title: Publish your software! A walkthrough of JOSS (Journal of Open Source Software) submission to publication
reasoning: This talk is about JOSS as a recognition venue for RSE work, addressing the profession-wide issue of evidencing RSE impact through publication.
abstract:
Helping researchers make better software is the main goal of the Research Software Engineer and it can take multiple forms, from providing training and advice to creating a complete research software. 
Unfortunately, while it is clear that software has become a predominant part of the scientific process, as found out by different surveys [1,2], the true impact of the RSE is sometimes hard to evidence. This lack of evidence is in part because purely scientific publications tend to leave little place for the software part of the research process while favouring the scientific results themselves.
In 2016, the Journal of Open Source Software [JOSS] was created to tackle this issue. JOSS is a peer reviewed academic journal created with the objective of publishing papers about the research software themselves, giving the RSE world a perfect route for impact. Since its creation, JOSS has published more than 2400 papers in multiple scientific domains supporting works on complex modelling problems, research experiments and instruments, software libraries, etc...
In this walkthrough, we give an overview of the types of submissions published in JOSS and demonstrate the full life-cycle of the JOSS process, from the submission of the software and paper, to the review process and the final publication. We will explain both sides of the coin: the submitter and reviewer's point of views.
[1]: Hettrick, S., et al, It’s impossible to conduct research without software, say 7 out of 10 UK researchers. https://www.software.ac.uk/blog/2016-09-12-its-impossible-conduct-research-without-software-say-7-out-10-uk-researchers.
[2]: https://stanford-rc.github.io/stanford-software-survey/2021/two-thousand-twenty/

title: Herb.jl: Teaching programs how to program

abstract:
Wouldn’t it be great if a computer could program itself? You simply tell it what you want, magic happens, and you have your program. While this is still a farfetched dream, here we will introduce you to Herb.jl, a Julia library that gets us a step closer to this big goal through program synthesis: the task of automatically generating programs from a given specification.

Herb.jl serves two main goals. First, it aims to provide a missing toolbox for developing new program synthesisers, which is currently missing in the community. Second, it aims to unify many different flavours of program synthesis under a joint framework, making existing program synthesisers easy to use on new problems.

In this talk we will give a high-level introduction to program synthesis. We will present Herb.jl and show how Julia facilitates the library development on one hand, but also algorithm speed and composability of the synthesis procedure.

We will also address the challenges of realising such a software project in an academic setting, where a mix of researchers, PhDs, students and RSEs contribute to the library.

title: SQLite for scientists
reasoning: This talk teaches general-purpose database tooling (SQLite, SQL, etlhelper) applicable across scientific domains, using volcanism data merely as an example. The subject is cross-cutting data management practice for researchers.
abstract:
Excel is not a database.  As such, it lacks the data integrity constraints and flexible analysis methods that databases provide.  Nevertheless, it is widely used across science to store and process tables of data.  The aim of this presentation is to use SQLite, which is an open source database used in billions of applications, to demonstrate how easy it can be to use a real database instead.

I will use data from the Global Volcanism Program to show how data are stored, queried, filtered and analysed using Structured Query Language (SQL) methods such as GROUP BY and JOIN.  I will also show how "relations" can be used to build a sample database that separates concepts such as collection site and avoids repetition.

The tooling around SQLite has improved greatly in the last decade.  In this presentation, I use DbBrowser for SQLite as a general front-end, QGIS for custom forms and Datasette for sharing data across a network.  Finally, I will introduce `etlhelper`.  This is a Python library that we have developed at the British Geological Survey to simplify data transfer into and out of databases (including SQLite).  This makes using SQLite in scripted workflows even easier.

title: Building a Secure and Productive TRE: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Proxy PyPI
reasoning: This talk is about a Trusted Research Environment - a cross-cutting platform/framework for handling sensitive data across research domains, not tied to a specific discipline. It's general-purpose infrastructure for researchers.
abstract:
How can we achieve the right balance between security and productivity in research with sensitive data?
The world is awash with data that can be used to provide insights that benefit society. However, much of this data is effectively unavailable for use by researchers due to privacy concerns.
Unlocking access to this data requires building trust with the custodians who safeguard the data and with society as a whole. Traditionally, this trust has been secured by a "security maximalist" approach, either by design, or through excessive caution.
Here, we share the lessons of 6 years of working with over 50 data providers to support access to sensitive data for research under a flexible framework of information governance and technical controls.

We've built an open source information governance framework and reproducibly-deployable, cloud-based Trusted Research Environment (TRE).
In this talk we discuss:
- Making governance and security controls explainable to data risk holders
- Using a tiered risk model to help achieve shared consensus
- Supporting researcher effectiveness
- Where security and usability _don't_ end up being a trade-off
- The things you *don't* need in a locked-down environment
- The value of sharing governance models and TRE design choices openly
- The power of collaborating as a community to address shared challenges

Drawing on our experience, we will set out what a good balance between competing concerns looks like, what we do differently to other TREs, and how you can get involved with both our work and the wider TRE community.

title: R Development Hackathon

abstract: The R programming language is widely used in statistics and data analytics. It first appeared in 1993, and its first stable (1.0.0) release was in 2000. It has been maintained by a motivated team of volunteers since its creation. To continue its widespread success, however, we need to ensure that we can maintain the maintainers of the R project. Recently, there has been a movement to upskill more members of the community in how to make contributions to R, in the form of the “R Contribution Working Group” (https://contributor.r-project.org/). One initiative of this group is the organisation of “R Dev Days” where people come together to contribute to the code and documentation that gets distributed in binary versions of R (base R, the recommended packages and the Windows/macOS GUIs). This hackathon will follow the format of these Dev Days, where current and novice contributors work collaboratively on selected issues, with the goal of making progress on these issues and learning more about the R Development process along the way.

title: Large language models surpass human experts in predicting neuroscience results
reasoning: This is about applying LLMs to neuroscience research prediction—a domain-specific application (BrainGPT tuned on neuroscience literature), making it Research, though the methodology is transferable.
abstract: Scientific discoveries often hinge on synthesizing decades of research, a task that potentially outstrips human information processing capacities. Large language models (LLMs) offer a solution. LLMs trained on the vast scientific literature could potentially integrate noisy yet interrelated findings to forecast novel results better than human experts. To evaluate this possibility, we created BrainBench, a forward-looking benchmark for predicting neuroscience results. We find that LLMs surpass experts in predicting experimental outcomes. BrainGPT, an LLM we tuned on the neuroscience literature, performed better yet. Like human experts, when LLMs were confident in their predictions, they were more likely to be correct, which presages a future where humans and LLMs team together to make discoveries. Our approach is not neuroscience-specific and is transferable to other knowledge-intensive endeavours. This work was supported by Microsoft, made possible through using ND A100 v4 series virtual machines on Microsoft Azure.
