reasoning: The talk centers on Trusted Research Environments (Data Safe Haven), a cross-cutting platform for secure data access used across research domains, plus surrounding processes and external factors.
abstract:
Data Science and machine learning are powered by data, and there is plenty of data today: many human activities are powered by software that generates large quantities of it.
While large datasets are constantly generated, putting them in the hands of the engineers and researchers, who can better exploit them, is not always easy. In domains like finance or health, data sensitivity and user privacy require a limited and controlled distribution of data assets.

Arguably, the gold standard for solving this data availability problem is placing datasets within trusted research environments (TREs). TREs are closed computational environments equipped with technical and process controls that enable secure data access to vetted researchers. The Research Engineering Team at the Turing uses a TRE software, our in-house developed Data Safe Haven, alongside our trusted research process to support academic projects of diverse sizes and domains.

We learned that while software and processes are pivotal to the success of a TRE initiative, there are other external critical factors that, if ignored, can derail an academic project. For example, placing data in a TRE comes with regulatory and legal obligations that need to be addressed way before onboarding the researchers into the system. Or dealing with researcher frustration when facing the necessary security controls imposed by platform and process. In this talk, we will rely on years of experience to describe these external factors, their influence on the success of a TRE initiative, and how we approach them at Turing.

We will discuss:
Enabling data-driven research with TREs.
Software and process: The essential factors of every TRE initiative.
External critical factors: Legal, financial, data management, usability, and others.
The Turing way of dealing with these factors, to ensure a successful TRE initiative.

title: Leveraging GitHub API Data to Evaluate Git and GitHub Training Outcomes
reasoning: This is about evaluating training outcomes for Git/GitHub training - focused on training effectiveness and skill development in the RSE community, not on a specific tool or research domain.
abstract:
A key challenge in evaluating the effectiveness of technical training (e.g., Git) is assessing the real-world application of learned skills. Post-training surveys offer one assessment method but suffer from limitations such as variable response rates and limited long-term evaluation. Tracking tool usage in natural settings offers continuous and more detailed insights into application but presents implementation challenges.
The 'Git & GitHub through GitKraken Client - From Zero to Hero!' training has been delivered by the RSE Sheffield team to over 300 participants since 2016. Importantly, a core component of this training involves participants creating and merging a pull request (PR) in a dedicated repository ('evolottery'/'collaborative_github_exercise'). This hands-on exercise, while not initially for evaluation, offers a unique opportunity for naturalistic tracking of training application. Utilizing the GitHub API, we can retrieve data on these PRs (username and date) to assess participants' subsequent Git and GitHub activity.
The poster will detail findings from analysis of this cohort. Specifically, presenting changes in Github activity over time relative to training completion, and exploring the adoption of other Git/GitHub features used in the training. Finally, we will discuss the limitations of these results specifically and our methodology more generally.

title: A Data Science Platform for the National Oceanography Centre and Beyond
reasoning: The talk describes a general-purpose JupyterHub-based data science platform deployable across infrastructures. Although built at an oceanography centre, the platform itself is domain-agnostic, addressing reproducibility, training, and cloud/HPC deployment for RSEs broadly.
abstract:
One of the common issues faced in the world of research software is "it worked on my machine". In this talk, we will present our efforts at the National Oceanography Centre (NOC) to solve this problem and make the task of writing shareable and reusable software easier by building an interactive Data Science Platform (DSP) based upon JupyterHub. The platform is accessed through a web browser and includes the Pangeo [https://pangeo.io/] stack along with popular machine learning libraries. In addition to a Jupyter notebooks interface we have integrated Matlab and a remote desktop service, removing the need for users to install these locally or rely on X forwarding/NoMachine/VNC.  
The DSP was first deployed on servers owned by NOC. We are employing cloud native technologies such as Kubernetes and S3 style object stores as the basis for much of our digital research infrastructure. This allows us to deploy instances of the DSP on commercial cloud and national computing facilities, providing a uniform user experience regardless of the underlying system. Where the DSP’s server is not powerful enough, we use Dask to enable access to high performance computing or cloud computing resources.  
In addition to providing a resource for developing and running research code, the platform is ideal for training. We use it regularly for Carpentries workshops since it provides all the software the learners require, resulting in a significant time saving during workshops, and allows ongoing access after the workshop.  
As well as a demonstration of this platform, we will present our experiences of deploying and running it, including lessons we have learnt along the way and our plans for its future.

title: AutoEmulate:  Python library for automatically creating accurate and efficient emulators of complex simulations.
reasoning: AutoEmulate is a general-purpose Python library for building ML emulators of simulations across disciplines, making it a cross-cutting software tool rather than domain-specific.
abstract: Physical systems are understood and developed through simulations. The complexity of these systems often results in costly and time-consuming simulations. Emulators (surrogate models) can approximate the solution of simulations at a fraction of the computational expense. However, building effective emulators typically requires significant machine learning (ML) expertise, posing a barrier for domain experts. To overcome this limitation, we present AutoEmulate, a Python package that automates the construction of the best emulator suited for a given simulation, employing state-of-the-art advancements in the field. AutoEmulate supports a wide range of emulator models as well as data preprocessing, calibration, and analysis methods. AutoEmulate’s user-friendly interface enables domain experts to deploy high-performance emulators with minimal ML expertise, offering a reliable solution for simulation-driven exploration across various disciplines.

title: pyonb: an open-source API and optical character recognition SDK for automated document-to-text conversion of clinical records
reasoning: pyonb is an OCR SDK designed primarily for clinical/medical records processing in UK hospitals. While the tool is content-agnostic, it is purpose-built for a specific domain (clinical/healthcare data extraction), making it Research-flavored, but the talk emphasizes architecture, deployment, and tool integration which is general software engineering.
abstract:
Optical character recognition (OCR) software is becoming increasingly prevalent with the expanding computational power and advancements in natural language processing, which enables reuse of previously untapped data due to the lack of tools for converting images into computer-readable text. Broadly, OCR is the analysis, recognition and extraction of text from documents. There are numerous open-source OCR software toolkits (Tesseract, Docling, olmOCR, PaddleOCR, Marker, Sparrow, MinerU, etc.) providing automatic conversion of images or filetypes such as PDF and DOCX into structured outputs.
Data storage is significantly heterogenous across and within UK hospitals. Medical data is often stored within data warehouses containing hundreds of millions of documents. This volume of data combined with the difficulty of information extraction from scanned documents represents a significant data processing challenge. From a research and innovation perspective, automatic text extraction of hospital documents enables innumerable possibilities such as improving diagnostics, clinical workflows and administrative processes. For example, AI methods can be applied to decades of untapped historical records to create prognostic models that cannot be developed in any other way. 
Here, we present pyonb (https://github.com/SAFEHR-data/pyonb), an open-source Python SDK for automated document-to-text conversion, designed for clinical processing (although it is content-agnostic so useable for any text extraction task). pyonb bundles multiple open-source OCR tools (including Marker, Sparrow, PaddleOCR, and more) with a central forwarding API for requesting which OCR tool to execute. pyonb is designed as a suite of containerised services which can be deployed on a server to retrieve documents from a data warehouse for automated OCR and text extraction.
In this work we describe:
the user requirements which motivated our design decisions
the software architecture
how developers can deploy the software and extend it to integrate their preferred OCR tool
the performance and processing speeds of a subset of OCR tools

title: JAX for Scientific Computing: Bridging the gap between performance, productivity and portability
reasoning: JAX is a general-purpose scientific computing/ML library; the talk focuses on its cross-cutting features for performance and portability, though examples come from specific domains like fluid mechanics and plasma physics.
abstract: In this talk, I will discuss the use of the JAX library for solving problems in scientific computing. After a brief discussion of the main features of the library, I will focus on how these features enable researchers to develop more efficient implementations of their scientific models that can run on both CPUs and GPUs and that can interface with machine-learning models seamlessly. I will show examples of open-source JAX-based solvers for a few problems across computational science and engineering and share personal experience of developing software for applications in fluid mechanics and plasma physics. Finally, I will discuss some limitations of the JAX library and issues and shortcomings that I have experienced.

title: Collaborative development of a performance analysis methodology
reasoning: This talk is about developing a general performance analysis methodology for HPC software development, applicable across domains. It's a cross-cutting software engineering practice, with community-building elements through workshops.
abstract:
Use cases of computationally intensive resources, such as High-Performance Computing (HPC), are increasingly diversifying with the advent of machine learning and the rise of the digital arts and humanities, while traditional HPC continues to push the boundaries and ask for more capability. This means we have a more demanding and diverse audience of HPC developers, and we therefore want to build a community on robust methods and practices for HPC use. Performance analysis must play an integral role in how developers use their software, because performant software allows researchers to do more research, but also to responsibly use the shared HPC resources economically and ecologically. This talk reports on findings from a series of workshops and investigative works undertaken at Durham University to develop a performance analysis methodology that is broad but nonetheless rigorous. Typically, performance analysis training begins with profiling and tracing tools. However, this can often leave developers using tools to generate performance data but without a strategy of how to systematically analyse this data or navigate through the space of analysis options. We propose a ‘methodology first’ approach, in which our use of tools is informed by our methodology, i.e., we want to plan our analysis and reach for the right tool for the job. It also comprises a clear roadmap of how to start an analysis and what steps to follow one by one. 
This methodology at the highest level is based on five performance topics: core, intra-node, inter-node, I/O and GPU. The work to develop this methodology has engaged HPC-focused software engineers to collaboratively design decision trees and metrics to probe these individual performance topics. One outlook of this work is to engage with broader communities to understand how these methodologies can be adapted to incorporate the latest HPC workflows including machine learning.

title: Deploying and Customising KerkoApp: a successful internship project
reasoning: The talk covers both a general-purpose tool deployment (KerkoApp - cross-cutting bibliographic search tool) and the experience/value of an RSE internship program. The internship/career pathway angle is strongly emphasized as a key takeaway, but the software deployment is also central.
abstract:
Have you or members of your institution been looking for an easy way to present a searchable collection of resources? KerkoApp is an open-source Python-based web application that provides an easy to use, searchable and browsable interface for bibliographic records stored in the Zotero reference management system. It is being used at the University of York to present a catalogue of the research outputs of a 5-year multi-institution plasma project (TDoTP) and as a community-driven resource for collating datasets and tools for researchers focusing on the human voice (YorVoice Catalogue).

The initial deployment and customisation of KerkoApp at York was the first project undertaken by our current year in industry RSE intern. It gave them the opportunity to learn aspects of a wide range of languages and technologies including virtual machines, Docker, Puppet, Python, Flask, Jinja, CSS, nginx and LLMs. They also developed their interpersonal and presentational skills through working closely with researchers on the TDoTP project and presenting the catalogue at the project's final advisory panel meeting.

Poster attendees will find out more about KerkoApp and how it has been deployed and customised at York. Attendees will also learn about the experiences of an RSE intern and the benefits that employing an RSE intern brings to the intern, the RSE team and the wider institution. This project demonstrates the value and benefits of establishing RSE career pathways and promoting RSE skills development within the context of DRI.

title: Carpentries Lesson on Intermediate Research Software Development
reasoning: This is about a training curriculum/course for RSEs, focused on community-building around training and recruiting contributors. It's profession-wide training infrastructure.
abstract: The Intermediate Research Software Development Course is now at the beta stage in the Carpentries Incubator. Along the path of its maturity, many pilot sessions have been conducted, asynchronous contributions made, and lessons learned as a result. A brief summary of the current status of the course will be displayed, including topics like successful delivery styles that have been used, alternate tooling options such as the popular VS Code IDE, and recent changes to the course content on software design and architecture. As course maintainers, we are always looking for new contributors, so a primary aim of this poster is to raise awareness of the course and its current status. Consequently, we will attract more interest from the RSE community to build a wider platform of support and increase uptake. To facilitate this, we will signpost routes and resources that new contributors can use to get involved.

title: Fluid: Towards Transparent, Explorable Research Outputs
reasoning: Fluid is a general-purpose programming language/tool for transparent visualization and reporting, applicable across research domains, supporting open science ergonomics.
abstract:
Although open science principles like FAIR data aim to make scientific results more accessible, intelligible and reusable, in practice “open”  usually just means that data sets and source code are available for download. The charts, figures and text used to present scientific claims remain difficult to interpret or challenge, even for experts. What can we do to build on today's baseline of best practices to address these more ergonomic needs?
Fluid is a new programming language designed to support transparent visualisation and reporting for web-based documents. Fluid provides a runtime  environment with built-in tracking of fine-grained data dependencies; this allows us to integrate data lineage information -- views of the relevant underlying data -- directly into charts and figures, through additional interactions. Selecting a graphical element in a chart can automatically reveal the relevant data, and highlight elements in other visualisations that use the same data.
This presentation will introduce Fluid's syntax and execution model, demonstrate the current tooling, and report on a user study exploring the impact of transparent visualisations on interpretability and trust. We will also demonstrate how to incorporate lineage queries into textual content. For example, if a paragraph of a climate report claims that under a particular emissions scenario, global warming of 2°C is “extremely likely” to be exceeded in the 20th century, a researcher can use Fluid to link key fragments of text to the underlying data and queries over those data sets, so that someone  interested in exploring the evidence base can drill into the underlying data without leaving the context of the report.
The session will be relevant to data scientists and research software engineers interested in how software infrastructure might help support the ergonomic goals of open science, at least for web-based documents. More information and interactive examples are available at https://f.luid.org.

title: gprMax + MPI: Large-scale open-source computational electrodynamics
reasoning: gprMax is a domain-specific tool for computational electrodynamics (GPR modelling in geophysics, archaeology, medicine), so it's Research. The MPI/HPC scaling work and ReFrame testing have cross-cutting Software relevance.
abstract:
gprMax is an open-source software package for computational electrodynamics. Designed with a general electromagnetic solver engine, it has a set of core features developed for modelling Ground Penetrating Radar (GPR) and can be used to model electromagnetic wave propagation in fields such as engineering, geophysics, archaeology, and medicine. gprMax is a Python codebase with performance-critical parts using Cython.
This poster showcases the impact of research software engineers on enabling scientific research. Before this project, gprMax simulations could run using a CPU solver parallelised using OpenMP or a GPU solver developed using the NVIDIA CUDA programming model. However, these solvers ran on a single CPU node or GPU, preventing the full utilisation of HPC systems and limiting models to those that fit in the memory of a single node. Our work dramatically increases the modelling capabilities of gprMax by adding a Message Passing Interface (MPI) domain decomposition to the CPU solver that divides models between multiple nodes/MPI tasks. This can reduce the time to results when running on a single node, but more importantly, enables researchers to scale the size and/or resolution of their electromagnetic simulations, allowing them to utilise HPC systems and explore new science.
Additional improvements of interest to the RSE community include a Python interface to support file formats for parallel I/O (VTKHDF), a new suite of regression tests built for HPC using the ReFrame framework, and work to create visualisations of the model geometry and resultant electromagnetic field to demonstrate the new functionality in an accessible way.

title: Discovering Academic Open Source:- Universities don't know how much they contribute to the OS ecosystem, why is this and what can we do about it?
reasoning: This BoF discusses measuring and recognizing open source contributions at universities, OSPOs, career incentives — a profession-wide policy/community topic.
abstract:
Open
Source is created and consumed everywhere. Many companies have good insights of
what open source code is developed, contributed and used internally. This is
not the case for universities. In recent years, researchers have released and
contributed to lots of open source software, mostly motivated by Open Science
movements (Open Data, FAIR principles, reproducibility networks), but
universities don’t know what activity is happening in their university or how
much impact that software is having.  
Moreover,
there may not be a motivation for researchers or students to share their open
source activity. For example, the impact of open source contribution may not
help their career progression as compared with research publications. 

In
this BoF session, participants will discuss what to consider when measuring
open source involvement (including beyond code) in a university or research
institution. We will examine what techniques are currently being employed to
measure open source activity by academic Open Source Program Offices (OSPOs)
globally, what are potential benefits and drawbacks of making this visible, and
efforts that are being put in place to recognise and reward the social and
economic impact of open source research outputs.

title: Towards a National Research Software Engineering Capability: evidencing the impact of RSEs
reasoning: This is about establishing a national RSE capability, evidencing RSE impact, and community/profession-building, focused on the A&H domain but addressing the RSE profession itself.
abstract:
We present an exciting new co-authored Roadmap outlining how to establish a national, people-centred Arts & Humanities (A&H) RSE Capability. Underpinned by a new evidence bank demonstrating the impact RSEs make on research, this work, though focused on one domain, has relevance across the research landscape.

We reflect on the process of creating these outputs, including the careful community management and design that motivated a stakeholder group of 40 co-authors. We also address how we responded to an unexpected but vital funder question: ‘Where is the evidence that RSEs are worth investing in?’ The evidence bank provides a compelling answer, detailing how RSEs organise, interpret, and find meaning in vast and complex data, enabling outputs, accelerating research, and even reducing costs.

The Roadmap acknowledges that infrastructure is both technical and social. Designed with a community of leaders and potential users, it responds to the need to avoid duplication by connecting and extending existing infrastructure. While rooted in A&H needs and challenges, it engages with the broader ecosystem, aiming for integration between domains rather than further separation. It is grounded in case studies that evidence existing impactful RSE capability models across A&H, cultural heritage, and social sciences and that highlight both the potential and need to scale: in terms of user communities, good practice, and innovation pathways. Crucially, the Roadmap also proposes a metascientific research effort to inform strategy, evaluate impact, and support the sector in adapting to evolving technologies and policies. All of this supports open scholarship practices to maximise impact, engagement, and value for money.

We close by inviting reflection on how other disciplines have contributed to the Roadmap’s development, and how they too can benefit from what it sets out.

title: Entity tagging and relation extraction from historical texts using deep learning
reasoning: This is a walkthrough on training transformer models for NER/RE specifically applied to digital humanities historical texts (Old Bailey Proceedings). It serves a specific research domain (digital humanities/history), making it Research, though the techniques themselves are general ML/NLP.
abstract:
The process of assigning metadata to spans of text in order to encode meaning, or “marking up”, has been central to digital humanities practice since before the field had a name. Thousands of person-hours have been devoted to this task, either performing the process entirely manually, or partially assisted by NLP software.

Since the 2010s, deep learning has profoundly impacted NLP, greatly expanding the range of language tasks which can be performed automatically or semi-automatically. Transformers in particular have improved the performance of tasks such as Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Relation Extraction (RE) to the point where it is plausible that markup tasks previously performed by skilled research assistants can, with appropriate training data, be automated or partially automated. The Digital Humanities Institute in Sheffield has been involved in many large scale markup projects over the past twenty-five years and amassed a huge tranche of potential training data for these tasks. To what extent can deep learning models accurately learn and replicate the work of the researchers who first tagged this material in the 2000s and 2010s?

This walkthrough will instruct participants in how to set up and train a transformer model to mark up defendants, crimes and verdicts in text from the Old Bailey Proceedings and correctly identify the relationships between them. It will also explore how to deduce the optimum training strategy for any similar markup task. For example, the number of ground truth human examples required to produce good results, or shortcuts such as using a partially trained transformer to assist a semi-automated workflow.

Ultimately this technology should allow relevant digital humanities projects to be delivered at lower cost and allocate more time and resources to data analysis rather than markup, promoting research excellence.

title: Green RSE SIG: Working together to reduce the environmental impact of research software
reasoning: This is about a Special Interest Group focused on community-building around green/sustainable RSE practices, advocacy, and profession-wide initiatives.
abstract:
The urgency of the climate crisis demands large scale reductions in emissions from across all sectors of society, including research.  Many funders and research institutions have committed to net zero pledges, that require large scale reductions in emissions, but as yet there is no clear pathway as to how these reductions become achievable.   
The Green RSE Special Interest Group is working to (1) identify and promote best practices for environmentally responsible research software, (2) collaborate on solutions that improve the efficiency of research code, reduce energy usage, and incorporate green practices into software lifecycle management, (3) advocate for green policies within research institutions, funding bodies, and broader communities, and (4) champion the role of RSEs in reducing the environmental impact of research software.
This session will hear from people working on this topic, to showcase the broad range of activities and share experiences. The intention this year is to highlight individuals who may not usually present on this but whose initiatives in their institutions can be interesting to the Green RSE community. There will also be an open discussion on the common challenges and opportunities this work brings. 
By bringing together a diverse and usually underrepresented group of voices, this session aims to spark discussion, surface ideas, and begin building a strong, connected community of practice around sustainable research software.

title: CATS: Climate-Aware Task Scheduler for environmentally conscious developers
reasoning: CATS is a general-purpose Python tool for scheduling tasks based on grid carbon intensity, applicable across domains—a sustainability/cross-cutting tool for RSEs.
abstract: The Climate-Aware Task Scheduler is a lightweight Python package designed to schedule tasks based on the estimated carbon intensity of the electricity grid at any given moment. This tool uses real-time carbon intensity data from the UK's National Grid ESO via their API to estimate the carbon intensity of the electricity grid, and schedules tasks at times when the estimated carbon intensity is lowest. This helps to reduce the carbon emissions associated with running computationally intensive tasks, making it an ideal solution for environmentally conscious developers. The source code can be found at https://github.com/GreenScheduler/cats.

title: From Lab to Launch: The evolving role of RSEs in driving sustainable and commercially viable digital solutions
reasoning: This talk focuses on the evolving role and expertise of RSEs in commercialization and translational research, addressing the profession itself rather than a specific tool or research domain.
abstract: Research Software Engineers (RSEs) have championed software development best practices and infrastructure standards to enable more reusable, sustainable and reproducible research tools. Their role continues to evolve, with these tools now driving societal impact through commercial and digital solutions. Today, RSEs, supported by Research Data Stewards (RDSs), provide both technical expertise including system design, data governance, quality assurance, and project management; and essential soft skills that underpin sustainable digital infrastructure. At University College London’s Centre for Digital Innovation (CDI) and Advanced Research Computing Centre (ARC), we see the growing need to broaden RSEs’ expertise to develop digital products that serve the public good and support commercially viable ventures. This shift involves understanding areas beyond coding, such as intellectual property, business model design, open-source innovation, data security, and technical leadership. In this talk, we will showcase how RSEs and RDSs are driving mission-led, globally focused solutions. We will also share real-world use cases and discuss the challenges in translating research into meaningful societal impact. We will cover:  (1) Overview of UCL CDI Impact Accelerator programme, (2) Research commercialisation landscape and translational research, (3) Difficulties that university spin-outs face compared to startups, (4) Role of RSE in technical support of academic entrepreneurs, (5) Overview of typical problems with producing research code and building product teams. We will conclude with a call to action to join our community of RSEs driving commercially viable solutions and invite everyone to explore and contribute to our workshop materials, available on our GitHub: CDI-Hub.

title: What support does research software need? Early lessons from the Research Software Maintenance Fund
reasoning: This talk is about a profession-wide funding initiative for sustaining research software, focused on policy/infrastructure for the RSE community rather than a specific tool or domain.
abstract:
Software is pervasive in modern research, used in every discipline and underpins many approaches including modelling and simulation; data management, analysis and visualisation; and experiment and laboratory control. Yet it can be difficult, even for widely used research software, to find resources for its maintenance, refactoring and community development, because the focus of much research funding is on novelty.

The Software Sustainability Institute is running the Research Software Maintenance Fund (RSMF), supported by the UKRI Digital Research Infrastructure programme, offering £4.8 million to support and sustain key research software, ensuring it remains reliable and accessible. This initiative is not only funding vital pieces of the research ecosystem but helps us understand what support research software needs to reduce technical debt and grow engagement and how we can effectively provide it.

In this short presentation, we’ll be presenting some early analysis of the types of activities that are being requested, putting them into the context of other research software funding initiatives, providing information on how the RSMF is operated, and getting feedback on what the community thinks is important to address next.

title: Project management beyond the process: How do RSE team leads learn what the role requires?
reasoning: This talk focuses on training and curriculum for RSE team leads, addressing the people/profession side—leadership skills, inclusive management, and team dynamics in research contexts.
abstract:
Research today cannot take place without Digital Research Infrastructure (DRI). But how are the teams that develop the research software which underpins DRI managed, and how do we ensure that those leading the teams have the right skills to make them effective and inclusive leaders?

There is a wealth of technical training material targeted at researchers, Research Software Engineers and other Research Technical Professionals (RTPs). Much of this material is open and freely accessible, and institutional RSE groups now play a large role in upskilling practitioners, as disseminated at RSECon. At the same time, through the UNIVERSE-HPC project, we are aware that this availability of training material doesn’t directly translate into a more skilled and capable workforce. 

A particular gap that has been identified is the lack of training materials aimed at teams developing research software, including helping those new to managing or leading diverse teams. There are a large number of resources on software project management, and general team management, but few which take into account the particular challenges of working in the research environment. 

This talk will present work that DRIFT (a follow-up to UNIVERSE-HPC) has done to identify the existing resources, approaches and audiences, and understand what adaptations might be required to be able to use existing materials in a research software engineering context. Starting with the goal of teaching project management skills as they can be applied to software development in research environments, we would like to get feedback from participants on a curriculum, in particular to identify any “hidden” objectives, such as enabling inclusive leadership and research integrity. This will contribute to an openly licensed course that will be piloted in 2026, focusing on the challenges of working with teams with different experience levels, promoting effective communication and knowledge transfer, and creating positive working environments.

title: Reasonable Performance Computing SIG (SIG-RPC): Help Identify and Document Performance Traps in Research Software
reasoning: This is about a SIG (community group) building a knowledge base around performance best practices. It's primarily community-building around the profession, with a strong software/performance technique component.
abstract:
Most research software is written by researchers who are not professionally trained programmers. This often leads to subtle but significant performance pitfalls—small coding choices, such as inefficient data structures, that can have an outsized impact on execution time. Even experienced developers struggle with performance issues, as language- and library-specific nuances are often learned through experience rather than formal documentation. Unreasonably slow research software harms the productivity of the researcher using it and wastes energy and shared resources (like HPC systems), which can harm the productivity of other researchers too.
The Reasonable Performance Computing SIG (SIG-RPC) was founded to build a community around the research, development, and advocacy of software performance best practices. A key part of this effort is curating a knowledge base of common performance traps and profiling tools to help researchers and developers write faster, more efficient code.
This workshop will introduce SIG-RPC and its knowledge base, guiding attendees through the process of contributing performance trap nominations and mini-guides based on their own expertise. Participants will engage in hands-on exercises such as:

Reviewing existing guides – Are they accessible to a broad audience, including non-experts?

Submitting new performance traps – Are there common pitfalls in your favourite language or library that haven’t yet been nominated or documented?

Contributing new guides – Can you document a performance trap from our backlog or your own experience?

All contributions will be published with attribution, helping to expand the community’s collective knowledge and supporting the development of future training materials on software performance best practices.

title: CapX – .NET Blazor-ing a trail? An(other) operational management tool for RSE groups
reasoning: CapX is a tool for RSE group operational management (capacity, timesheets, competency tracking) — it serves the RSE profession as a population, but also discusses Blazor as a web technology choice. The tool itself is about managing RSE teams (community/profession), but framed as a software walkthrough.
abstract: Whether you are leading a team of a few RSEs or managing a large department full of all manner of digital research technical professionals, capacity management is an essential activity. That is, knowing what everyone is assigned to work on, at what percentage, and for how long. The “spreadsheet of doom” used to play “Assignment Tetris” was an ineffective tool for the purpose, and so Capacity eXtended (CapX) was developed. However, it didn’t stop there. Frustrated by the lack of frictionless access to good quality data related to people and projects, the CapX data model started to grow, connecting information across the full research lifecycle. CapX now features workload model management for all staff, a competency framework to track development, timesheets, project cost tracking and a secure API so RSEs can build their own tools on top of the database. This walkthrough will demonstrate the features and provide insights into the supporting processes that underpin them. Furthermore, it will discuss the choice of .NET Blazor as its foundation and present as case for why Blazor might be an ideal choice to help diversify your RSE web technology pool.

title: Let's stop pretending to be unicorns!
reasoning: This talk is about RSE identity, self-perception, and collaboration culture within the profession—clearly about people and the profession.
abstract:
Research software engineers as unicorns: Here comes the magical RSEcorn, flying in, solving all your problems! 
Or does it?
The narrative of the omnipotent RSE which can be used "plug&play" in research projects might be useful for lobbying for recognition and funding, but is problematic for working relationships with researchers. Not only can it lead to frustrations on both sides, it is also the perfect ingredient for imposter syndrome for the RSE.
This talk is questioning the way that we, as the RSE community, tend to view and present ourselves, and how this develops into an unhealthy "us vs. them" culture in some parts of the community. 
I also want to highlight where alternative collaboration patterns already exist, and propose an alternative image for ourselves within the wider research community.

title: FAIR2 for research software: developing a FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable) and reproducible research software training programme
reasoning: This submission is about developing a training programme to teach FAIR principles for research software, focusing on capacity building and skill development across the researcher community. It centres on training and profession-wide initiatives rather than a specific tool or research domain.
abstract:
Recently there has been growing recognition that research software, defined as “source code files, algorithms, scripts, computational workflows and executables that were created during the research process or for a research purpose”1, should adhere to the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable and Reusable) principles2, as well as meeting broader open research goals such as reproducibility. The FAIR guidelines for research software (FAIR4RS) provide a framework for the development of FAIR research software1. However, many researchers require additional support to meet these guidelines. Training in the FAIR4RS principles is needed to promote the uptake of FAIR research software practices3.
The University of Sheffield Research Software Engineering team and collaborators developed a modular training programme to support researchers in applying FAIR principles and open research practices to their research software. Topics are offered as separate modules which can be selected according to an individual’s learning goals. We aim to motivate and equip participants with the skills and knowledge needed to create and publish FAIR research software, to meet our goal to support research excellence at the university by enhancing capacity for producing high quality, efficient and sustainable research software.
So far the programme has attracted over 200 registrations and 150 attendees across the University of Sheffield, and provided over 40 hours of training, from software lifecycle planning and licensing to packaging and publishing software. Course materials have been developed as open educational resources under Creative Commons licensing. Feedback from participants indicates that this training is timely and relevant to researchers’ needs.
1 Barker et al., 2022, ‘Introducing the FAIR Principles for Research Software’.
2 Wilkinson et al., 2016, ‘The FAIR Guiding Principles for Scientific Data Management and Stewardship’.
3 Barker et al., 2024, ‘The FAIR for Research Software Principles after two years’.

title: Improving diversity and inclusivity in RSE: From understanding to practical tools.
reasoning: This workshop centers on diversity and inclusivity in the RSE profession, addressing people and community-building rather than tools or domain-specific software.
abstract: This workshop invites RSEs, team leaders, and community members to learn more about ongoing diversity and inclusivity work at the UK Software Sustainability Institute (SSI) and gain practical tools and techniques to improve diversity in their own contexts. Firstly, we will present key findings from the Inclusive RSE research project which seeks to understand the experiences of underrepresented groups in RSE and work towards practical solutions. We will then ask for your feedback on this project: What resonates within our research? What do you feel is missing? Where do you think we should go next? Following this, we will share actions taken within the SSI’s Fellowship programme to improve diversity, and discuss how these strategies can be adapted to RSE recruitment and community building more broadly. Finally, we will share a scenario-based tool designed to help individuals and teams reflect on and improve inclusivity in RSE. You will have hands-on experience with the tool, guidance on adapting it to tailor it for your own setting, and space to share approaches that have worked within your own institutions. By the end of the session, you will be equipped with new insights, practical strategies, and a connection to people committed to promoting inclusive RSE practice.

title: AMD GPUs for Scientific Computing: Reviewing the Software Ecosystem & Developer Experience
reasoning: This talk reviews GPU computing ecosystems (AMD vs NVIDIA) as a cross-cutting tooling/platform concern relevant to RSEs broadly, not tied to a specific scientific domain.
abstract:
At present, NVIDIA dominates the consumer and scientific GPU markets with a market share above 80% for discrete GPUs. AMD GPUs look to be the most viable short-term competitor, but just how viable are they for scientific computing right now? 

In this talk, we will explore the state of the AMD GPU computing ecosystem and compare it against the NVIDIA ecosystem in terms of usability, library availability, support and performance. These aspects are explored through a publicly available suite of implementations of fundamental GPU algorithms e.g. parallel searches and sorts. These are implemented using both NVIDIAs CUDA and AMDs equivalent, HIP/ROCm.

We will also discuss the developer experience of porting a more substantial code which is representative of a scientific computing application. Through this, feature availability is reviewed, looking at things such as atomic operations. In addition we review the state of AMDs compute library ecosystem, discussing the existence and/or effectiveness of equivalents to Thrust, CUB etc. 

Finally, we take a look at the viability of tools which offer automatic conversion of code from CUDA to HIP/ROCm.

title: Automated CI/CD with GitHub Actions, starting from scratch
reasoning: This is a walkthrough on general-purpose CI/CD practices using GitHub Actions, applicable across domains.
abstract:
Have you ever developed a piece of code, pushed it to a GitHub repository main branch, and then moved on to other things? How do you ensure that the code remains functional in a few months’ time, when various dependencies have updated? How do you go about assigning a version number to allow clear traceability of issues for your users? And once you have released a version, how do you go about automatically deploying that to a package repository; ensuring easy installation for your userbase? 
In this walkthrough, we will take a basic software tool as an example and answer these questions (and more) by incrementally building up Continuous Integration/Continuous Delivery (CI/CD) workflows using the ubiquitous GitHub Actions platform. 
Workflows will be developed in a live demonstration. Among other things, we will show you how to automate testing, packaging and deployment for a range of triggers (e.g. updates to a pull request). We will explore the Marketplace for some of the reusable actions that you can embed in your own workflows. We will also talk about some of the pitfalls you will encounter if you don’t release regular versions of your code, and make the case for using CI/CD regardless of the size and reach of your codebase.

title: Unit Testing in Fortran
reasoning: This is a walkthrough on unit testing tools for Fortran—a cross-cutting software engineering practice applicable across domains, not tied to a specific research field.
abstract:
Unit testing and testing in general is widely accepted as essential for any reputable modern software. However, it is common to still find Fortran codebases with large communities that contain little to no testing implemented. Where testing has been implemented, this is often in the form of a small suite of end-to-end regression tests. Whilst these regression tests are a great first step, we can do better! There are already several open-source tools to choose from when it comes to unit testing in Fortran, so there is no time like the present to start testing.  
In this walkthrough, we will look at how to set up and write unit tests for Fortran code in a subset of the available tools (pFUnit, test-drive and Veggies) using two build systems (CMake and Fortran Package Manager). Key concepts will be explained and pre-written examples provided. Users will also get a chance to try writing their own Fortran unit tests in a pre-configured repository. Examples will cover testing both serial and parallelised Fortran using OpenMP and MPI, highlighting any key differences.

title: How AI is Changing DevOps: From Code Suggestions to Auto-Remediation
reasoning: This talk is about AI-powered DevOps tooling—code suggestions, CI/CD optimization, auto-remediation—which are cross-cutting software engineering practices applicable across domains.
abstract:
As DevOps matures, we're witnessing a paradigm shift—one where artificial intelligence is no longer just an enhancement, but a driving force. In this talk, I’ll share lessons and insights from over a decade and working on large-scale cloud-native systems at AWS, where I’ve had a front-row seat to how AI is fundamentally reshaping the DevOps lifecycle.
We'll explore how AI-powered tools are moving beyond simple static analysis to provide contextual code suggestions, intelligent pull request reviews, and even predictive CI/CD pipeline optimizations. More importantly, we’ll dive into the emerging field of auto-remediation—where AI models trained on historical telemetry and incident data can detect anomalies, pinpoint root causes, and initiate corrective actions autonomously.
This session is designed for practitioners, leaders, and architects who want a strategic yet hands-on view of how AI is changing the way we build, deploy, and operate software in the cloud—today and in the years to come.

title: Pre-commit to better code
reasoning: This is a walkthrough about pre-commit, linters, and type checkers — general-purpose software engineering tooling applicable across domains.
abstract: In this walkthrough, I will walk through using pre-commit to make your code better. Pre-commit, along with automated linters and type checkers, enforces guidelines on every commit, from stylistic issues such as whitespaces and indents, to automatically checking your code for common errors, such as missing imports or incorrect types. In collaborative projects, pre-commit can be invaluable in ensuring that the codebase is of a uniform quality.

title: From open science goals to technical implementation: Enabling sustainable data sharing for a research team
reasoning: This talk describes RSEs supporting a specific research team (socio-ecological sustainability) to share a domain-specific dataset, including building a companion R package and dashboard. The work is tied to a particular research project, though it also illustrates general RSE practices around sustainability and open science.
abstract:
In this talk, we will present how as RSEs we helped a research team achieve part of their open science goals.
A group of researchers studying the generation of scientific knowledge for socio-ecological sustainability sought to share with the public a 5.5-million-row dataset they created during a three-year project in an accessible and engaging way. While their initial expectation was to create a dashboard using Shiny for R, it soon became clear that the nature of the dataset, the financial constraints of the project, and the target audience required a broader approach.
During the talk, we will discuss how we approached the process of understanding their needs, managing expectations, and devising a sustainable solution. We will also share some of the technical decisions made to that end, such as restructuring the data for efficient querying, precomputing summary tables, implementing interface logic that dynamically adjusted the level of granularity based on user interaction, and developing a companion R package. These design decisions balanced usability with long-term maintainability, ensuring that the tool could remain available beyond the end of the research funding.
This experience illustrates how RSEs contribute not only code, but also strategic thinking that bridges open research goals with the technical realities of implementation. By aligning design decisions with open science principles and practical constraints, RSEs can help ensure that research outputs are not just published, but also usable, reusable, and impactful over time.

title: rplaywright: Bridging Playwright to R for Reproducible Web Automation in Research
reasoning: rplaywright is a general-purpose R package bridging Playwright for web automation, applicable across research domains rather than tied to a specific discipline.
abstract:
Dynamic web content plays an important role in research, from accessing public dashboards to automating testing workflows. However, R users face challenges when working with JavaScript-heavy websites, as most available tools rely on static HTML scraping or browser automation approaches that can be difficult to integrate smoothly into R workflows.
To address these challenges, rplaywright (https://erikaris.github.io/rplaywright/) was developed to integrate the R environment with Microsoft’s Playwright, a browser automation framework used across multiple programming languages. The package enables automated interaction with Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit browsers, operating in either headless or visible modes. It supports tasks such as navigating web pages, scrolling through dynamically loaded content, completing online forms, and extracting information from sites that update dynamically. Features including automatic waiting for page components, handling of infinite scrolling, and reliable interaction with dynamic interfaces facilitate reproducible workflows for research involving web resources.
rplaywright facilitates the seamless integration of dynamic web content into R-based research workflows, supporting scalable and reproducible data collection from interactive web portals. The project originated as part of the rOpenSci Champions Program, emphasising open development and community-driven technical mentorship. The package is suitable for workflows involving interactive data portals, social media platforms, and dynamic dashboards, enabling researchers to programmatically navigate pages, interact with filters, and extract underlying data for analysis. This poster will present the architecture of rplaywright, highlight key design considerations, demonstrate integration with popular R packages for streamlined analysis, and explore how cross-language tools can extend R’s capabilities to enhance research outcomes.

title: Create impactful scientific visualisations from your laptop*!   (* also requires access to HPC)
reasoning: Brr is a general-purpose tool for using Blender with HPC for scientific visualization, applicable across research domains rather than tied to a specific discipline.
abstract:
BlenderRemoteRender (Brr) is a client-server tool for working with Blender, specifically in a research context. Blender is a free and powerful 3D design and rendering toolkit. Although it is used more and more by the research community for producing high quality scientific visualisations, its primarily target is 3D artists. One of the key workflow difference being that researchers, unlike 3D artists and studios, may not have access to powerful rendering hardware locally or render farms. They however usually have remote access to High Performance Computing (HPC) resources setup with a job scheduler. Brr allows researchers to work on their scenes and visualisations locally on a light client while seamlessly connecting to HPC resources and submitting jobs via their scheduler to render images and animations. Because animation rendering is an embarrassingly parallel problem - each frame being independent of each other - Brr maximises Blender's parallel performance by dynamically scheduling frames to single GPUs or single CPU nodes and working with multiple nodes.
In practice, Brr is composed of a Blender addon on the client side and a Zero MQ server both implemented in Python. The server is tasked with receiving configuration and data files from the client, submitting jobs to a queue system (like slurm) and sending back progress status and rendered images.

title: Deploying a Web Application with Kubernetes, A Beginner's Guide
reasoning: Hands-on workshop teaching Kubernetes deployment, a general-purpose cross-cutting technology for RSEs. Mentions a SIG but the focus is the tool/technique tutorial.
abstract:
The academic world is asking for more web-based software to make research more accessible to both researchers and the public. There are many challenges with writing, maintaining and deploying web services, so how as an RSE can we make this journey easier. Cloud-Native technology (Kubernetes) is a very easy and stable way for researchers to deploy cloud based web applications and can be run on everything from a local laptop, Raspberry Pi or HPC reducing the need for a Cloud provider to run your web apps.  This workshop is designed for new starters to Kubernetes who wish to have a practical demonstration of how this technology works and how to apply it in their fields.
 We will provide a hands-on tutorial of how:
 To deploy a simple web application via Minikube
To make updates to your website
Kubernetes can automatically recover when there are underlying problems.
This workshop is for RSEs of all career stages who are interested in web applications, DevOps or deployment. The aim is for participants to come away with a working understanding of Kubernetes and the tools needed to continue to work on this in their own time and maybe bring the technology into part of their working practice. 
This workshop is run by the Cloud-Native SIG, a new special interest group, working to promote the use of Cloud-Native techology in RSE.

title: A Context for Requirements Handling in an Agile Workflow
reasoning: This talk discusses agile methodology and requirements handling practices applicable to RSE teams broadly - a cross-cutting software engineering practice rather than a domain-specific tool. It also touches on team workflow management.
abstract:
When King’s Digital Lab (KDL), an RSE unit based in the Faculty of Arts and Humanities at King’s College London, began operations in 2016 we quickly adopted the industry-standard DSDM Agile methodology. Its emphasis on a fixed-time-and-cost basis with flexibility on features aligns well with the grant-funded projects work we commonly do. Our SDLC includes DSDM-recommended steps and documentation which we have found very helpful. However, because we have small solution development (SDT) teams each working on several projects simultaneously, workflows can be complex and it has been challenging to fully and consistently follow Agile precepts, especially with respect to handling project requirements. 
We like the theory of moving from initial high-level requirement descriptions to greater specificity via iterative development but in practice have found that while a typical Agile try/asses/adjust/try again fosters creativity and refinement in implementation it also brings a constant risk of confusion and inefficiency for the SDT. We have come to see that fast-paced iteration demands a fixed context: something consistent, intuitive, and convenient that allows both SDT and project partners to produce and keep track of evolving requirement descriptions and the constantly moving parts - discussions, decisions, task creation, etc. - that surround them.  ‘Context’ here is not quite an approach (as, for instance, Specification by Example), or a formalized set of practices (like the Requirements Development & Management Practice Area of CMMI), or a purpose-built software tool (e,g. Altium 365) but might incorporate aspects from any or all those things. 
Drawing from our experience at KDL this talk will firstly discuss specific issues in requirements handling which can thwart Agility and frustrate all parties in a project. It will then set out aims, principles and practical considerations pertinent to a fixed context that facilitates rapid iteration in an environment of multiple complex workflows.

title: HPC Carpentry
reasoning: This is about training materials and curriculum development for HPC skills, part of a community-led teaching program (The Carpentries). It centers on profession/training rather than a specific tool or research domain.
abstract:
The HPC Carpentry project aims to develop highly interactive workshop training materials to empower novices to effectively leverage HPC to solve scientific and technical problems in their domains. This talk provides an overview of the project and its history, explores the content and delivery of HPC Carpentry workshops, and summarises the community's plans for the future. 
Modeled after The Carpentries training programs, the project’s goal is to develop foundational HPC skills and a sense of empowerment, rather than expertise. The workshop setting provides learners with hands-on experience that elicits confidence working with HPC systems and provides sufficient vocabulary to make subsequent self-study more effective.
In a major milestone, the steering committee is leading HPC Carpentry through the formal incubation process to become an official lesson program of The Carpentries, a global community teaching essential data and software skills for research. If adopted, HPC Carpentry will join the existing Software, Data, and Library Carpentry programs. This achievement is the product of significant work over the past several years, incorporating valuable materials from many contributors.
Our most recent focus has been developing materials for a user workshop. We begin with an introduction to the command-line shell (using Software Carpentry’s Unix Shell lesson), followed by our Introduction to HPC lesson, covering remote access and resource management. We end with a newly developed lesson on HPC workflow management, which walks learners through the execution of a scaling study on an HPC system, emphasizing both the benefits and limitations of the system for domain applications. This workshop program was recently run in full at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory.
Future plans include building a developer workshop, reconnecting with disparate contributors, and engaging with the broader community through regular open conference calls and outreach.

title: Developing and Leading Regional RSE Communities
reasoning: Workshop about building and leading regional RSE communities, organized by a SIG—clearly about people and profession.
abstract:
Are you leading, wanting to develop, or keen to join a regional group? In this workshop we want to discuss the value of regional groups, as well as challenges in starting, building up and maintaining momentum in those communities which fall half-way between institutional RSE hubs and national associations. With a mix of talks and discussions we will aim to extract best practices and not-so-great experiences, as well as giving people the opportunity to make connections to other community leaders.

The workshop will start with a number of talks where attendees will hear about the experiences (successful and not) of participating in and running regional groups. We will then facilitate an open and honest discussion where we will trade ideas and give advice. We hope to cover maintaining community engagement, regional meetups, regional funding as well as any ideas brought forward by the community.

At the end, attendees will be better prepared, connected and motivated to contribute to their regional group. They will gain an increased understanding of the value of these groups and where they stand in the RSE community hierarchy.

This workshop is organised by the Regional RSE Groups Special Interest Group.

title: Reflections on cross-cutting software tools born out of project work
reasoning: The talk reflects on developing FTorch, a cross-cutting tool for ML/Fortran interop, but the core message is about how RSEs identify and nurture cross-cutting software from domain projects—a profession/practice reflection. It straddles Software (the tool itself) and Community (RSE role and growing software).
abstract:
RSEs regularly collaborate on time-bounded projects, with code ownership remaining with researchers. Sometimes, however, such collaborations lead to the development of cross-cutting digital research infrastructure with potential for impact beyond a single project or domain.
How can RSEs identify and nurture these pieces of software, and how can they use their unique position in research to drive these interconnections?

ICCS RSEs work with climate scientists to improve the functionality and sustainability of climate modelling code. Much of this is written in Fortran, which remains relevant due to continued updates to the language standards and compilers, and considerable societal inertia, but lacks native support for machine learning (ML). With hybrid modelling being a popular research topic, a common request from collaborators is to facilitate inter-operation of their codebases with the popular ML package PyTorch. As a result we developed the FTorch interface. Given the cross-cutting nature of ML inter-operation, FTorch was spun out of the original project as a fully-fledged package in its own right and has since been deployed in several other projects and domains.

In this talk, we reflect on our experiences developing FTorch. We discuss the decision to spin FTorch out beyond the original collaboration, and the subsequent journey to become an independent package developed and maintained by our team. Early on we faced the challenge of developing FTorch in ‘non-project time’ and managing it in-house (something not generally within ICCS’ remit for project work). We subsequently secured FTorch-specific funding to support development, promotion, and collaboration. Finally, we discuss how the unique role of the RSE is well suited to spotting opportunities for interconnected research.

We hope that the talk will inspire attendees to focus on cross-cutting software that they have developed in their team and provide useful tips for how to grow such software into fully-fledged projects.

title: The End of Front-End: Delivering Software via LLMs and the Model Context Protocol
reasoning: This talk introduces a general-purpose protocol/technique (MCP) for delivering software via LLMs, applicable across research domains rather than tied to a specific discipline.
abstract:
What if the future of software delivery didn’t involve a user interface at all? With the rise of large language models (LLMs), we’re entering a new era where software can be consumed through natural conversation, not clicks. In this walkthrough, I’ll introduce the Model Context Protocol (MCP)—a new way to expose real-time, typed, dynamic data to LLMs, enabling them to act as intelligent, conversational front-ends for research software.
I’ll demonstrate how to build a simple MCP server that exposes live data and commands to an LLM, transforming a traditional API into a human-friendly interaction. Along the way, we’ll look at what problems this approach is suited for, how it compares to conventional apps, and what design patterns are emerging.
This session is designed for data scientists, engineers and researchers curious about combining conversational AI with real-world data and delivery workflows.

title: Green Research Software Engineering for Beginners
reasoning: Introduces green software engineering concepts and tools for RSEs broadly, covering cross-cutting sustainability practices and tooling applicable across domains.
abstract:
This poster introduces foundational green software engineering concepts collated specifically for Research Software Engineers (RSEs) at the beginning of their sustainability journey. With computational research increasingly driving scientific discovery, understanding the environmental impact of research software has become crucial. Research computing, particularly high-performance computing (HPC) consumes significant energy resources, making sustainable practices essential. 
We first highlight major scientific research fields that consume large amounts of compute power. 
We then identify key energy-intensive compute processes including CPU utilisation, memory management, disk operations, and continuous integration/deployment pipelines that represent significant areas for optimisation. 
The poster presents practical monitoring tools such as `CodeCarbon` for tracking machine learning model emissions and `AIWattch` for measuring large language model’s (LLM) environmental impacts during browser-based interactions. 
We introduce various metrics for evaluating software energy efficiency, e.g. energy consumption per function, water usage considerations, and lifecycle assessment approaches. 
By identifying emission scope in terms of direct (Scope 1), indirect energy-related (Scope 2), and value chain (Scope 3) impacts, we enable RSEs to make environmentally informed development decisions. 
The poster advocates for GREENER software engineering principles that promote awareness and collaborative action toward sustainable development practices.

As use of artificial intelligence and machine learning applications is booming across research domains, this introduction provides guidance for professionals seeking to minimise the environmental footprint of their increasingly computation-intensive work.

title: The KODAQS Toolbox: An Open Educational Resource for Ensuring Data Quality
reasoning: This is a domain-specific (social sciences) educational toolbox for data quality, but it's also a general framework for educational content. The primary focus is a tool built for social science research data quality, making it Research, with strong Software/Community (educational) aspects.
abstract:
Valid conclusions can only be drawn when data meets rigorous quality standards, and when researchers are equipped with the appropriate tools and expertise to assess them. Ensuring data quality has become particularly important within the social sciences due to increasingly complex research settings, a declining willingness to participate in surveys, and the growing reliance on automated and scalable evaluation of available data. To this end, we present the KODAQS Data Quality Toolbox, developed as part of the BMBF/EU-funded Competence Center for Data Quality in the Social Sciences (KODAQS).
The KODAQS Toolbox provides tools and tutorials on conducting key data quality analysis to help social scientists evaluate and improve the quality of their research data. The Toolbox covers three main data types: 1) survey data, 2) digital behavioral data, and 3) survey data linked with data from other sources, recognizing that challenges for data quality differ greatly for these data types.
At its core, the KODAQS Toolbox employs containerized environments to render literate programming-based contributions from open repositories into HTML pages as well as downloadable Jupyter Notebooks, Quarto files, and PDFs, ensuring the reproducibility of its materials. As an educational platform, the Toolbox lowers entry barriers for learners by providing reusable code, embedded video tutorials, sample datasets, self-assessments, and downloadable source files – all designed to support hands-on learning. In addition, it incorporates Binder-based interactive execution environments that allow users to run the learning materials directly in their browser without requiring complex setup.
The underlying open-source framework of the Toolbox allows straightforward integration of new tools and tutorials, making it an ideal platform for contributors to share their content. Beyond its immediate use, the Toolbox serves as a transferable model, demonstrating how modular, open, and reproducible content can be effectively aggregated to support a wide range of research domains.

title: Towards Cloud-Native Workflows for Environmental Data: Lessons from NOC and UKCEH
reasoning: The talk discusses cloud-native data workflows, object storage, Zarr/Kerchunk formats - generally applicable techniques, though motivated by environmental data domains (oceanography, ecology). The techniques themselves are cross-cutting and applicable to any large gridded dataset.
abstract:
Scientific datasets are continuing to increase in size. Traditional methods of data analysis are struggling with the increased local storage and compute resources required. As a result, a transition to cloud-based technologies and ways of working is becoming increasingly necessary. This talk shares the ongoing collaboration between the UK’s National Oceanography Centre (NOC) and the UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology (UKCEH) to explore management, sharing and analysis of large gridded environmental datasets based in the cloud. Our goal is to make the transition to working with datasets on the cloud as easy as possible for researchers.
We will focus on three key areas: object storage: what it is and why we are using it, cloud-native data formats and how we convert between them at scale, and interfaces for visualising and working with the data.
We store our data in object storage systems using Zarr and Kerchunk formats, which support massively-parallel access over the web and thus scalable computations. We’ve tested different ways to convert data, and will share what works well and what doesn’t. 
Using these formats come with its own set of challenges however. Key amongst these is the requirement that data is split into chunks. Chunk size strongly influences speed of data processing and visualisation but chunk sizes that are good for scientific analysis are not good for visualisation. We will share how we have attempted to mitigate this and other related challenges.  
We’ll show benchmarks comparing different methods and chunking strategy performance on the data conversion, simple scientific analyses and the tile-server visualisation, and share successes, challenges and tips that folk can take away from our work so far. We hope it will help others who are thinking about or working towards making their data systems more cloud-ready.

title: From code to contributions: exploring open source culture in academia
reasoning: This workshop focuses on the culture, recognition, and reward structures around open source contributions in academia—a profession-wide issue about people and incentives, not a specific tool or research domain.
abstract:
"It is a truth universally acknowledged that a code repository with an open source license must be in want of an extra maintainer." - Jane Austen, probably. 

While academic researchers and research technical professionals rely heavily on open source tools and software, and open research policies increase the amount of codebases available globally, contribution patterns remain uneven, with maintenance work often undervalued within academic reward structures. This workshop forms part of a larger 2025 SSI Fellowship projecct examining the current culture of open source contributions in the academic landscape and considering opportunities to incentivise, reward, and recongise the collective work of maintaining 
Participants will share personal experiences of open source contributions, and collectively analyse barriers to sustainable participation. They will also hear from groups currently working to actively promote open source contributions at their organisations, before brainstorming and developing practical proposals for effective support for open source contributions within academic settings. 
Participants will leave with both individual action commitments and collective strategies to enhance the recognition, support, and sustainability of open source contributions in academic environments.

title: An overview of the DisCouRSE Network+ grant: Developing a Community of Leaders in RSE and related professions
reasoning: This talk is about a grant developing leaders and community across RSE and related digital research technical professions, focused on careers, training, and profession-wide initiatives.
abstract:
I will introduce our newly funded UKRI Network+ grant, covering what we're aiming to accomplish in the next three years, and how we would like the whole community to get involved!
Scaling and sustaining the impact of digital Research Technical Professional (dRTP) communities like ours requires developing leaders who have an amplifying effect. Our central premise is to build from the critical mass of the UK RSE community, connecting and training cohorts of leaders, who can use our flexible fund to advance the skills and careers of all digital RTPs (not just RSEs). Much work has already been done, but opportunities are varied across role types and locations. Most success has been achieved through related professions working together, not by treating RSEs as a special case. We therefore seek to identify and expand such best practice, build stronger connections between those facing similar challenges, across sectors, and thereby make greater impact more rapidly. We are also investing in developing the Digital Research Competencies Framework to inform what training is needed for leaders, and partnering with existing experts to develop and deliver this at scale.
This talk will give a brief overview of the project and launch our first flexible funding call for proposals. We will distribute £1,000,000 as seed funding in multiple rounds over the next 3 years. I will describe the types of submission we are looking for (e.g. pilot projects, workshop series, training programmes, and the like) and how to apply for funding.
Related sessions with more interaction include 123, 127, and the training satellite day on Friday.

title: ConveRSE - Let's Talk About Mental Health
reasoning: This talk centers on mental health in the RSE profession, a community/profession-wide concern, and introduces a hub for resources aimed at RSEs and RTPs.
abstract:
As part of my Software Sustainability Institute (SSI) Fellowship, I’ve been looking for ways to support mental health in the research software community. 1 in 4 adults experience mental health problems each year, and in 2022, Dave Horsfall conducted a survey which showed that a range of issues are common among Research Software Engineers (RSEs). This is hardly surprising, as working as an RSE or Research Technical Professional (RTP) presents a unique set of challenges; we have to deal with context and technology switching, impostor syndrome, limited career opportunities and recognition, on top of software development being notorious for burnout and… well, everything going on in the world right now! If not properly managed, it can be a recipe for mental health disaster, as I know only too well!
In this talk, I will tell the story of how I became a father in lockdown, how it led to burnout and an anxiety attack, and how that experience motivated me to apply for the Fellowship. I will explain why I believe it is essential to continue the conversation around mental health, to create an environment where people can discuss mental health in the workplace, and why it’s better to address issues before they turn into larger problems. I will look at what we can practically do to support mental health among RSEs (and those in similar professions), including some advice, best practices and other things I’ve learned from telling my story and discussing mental health at various events over the last couple of years. Finally, I will introduce ConveRSE - a new online hub for mental health information, projects and resources aimed at RSEs and RTPs - and encourage people to get involved so we can work together to create a better future for ourselves and our colleagues.

title: Quick tips for making your software outlive your job
reasoning: This talk addresses software sustainability practices and resilience of research software in the face of personnel loss—a profession-wide concern about people, careers, and infrastructure, sourced via a ReSA Task Force.
